title: An Invitation from Molly

the_party.text:
The Royal Pigeon Inn has never looked more respectable. Its polished corridors, velvet carpets, and discreetly attentive staff seem designed to assure wealthy travelers that nothing undignified has ever happened within its walls.

On the way upstairs, you remind yourself to be mature, considerate, and above all prepared for whatever Molly has in mind. _Naturally._ The fact that you have adjusted your collar three times is merely a coincidence.

Molly opens the door with a brilliant smile. "You're here! Come in, come in!"

Her room makes a brave attempt to challenge the inn's reputation.

The chairs have been pushed aside, cushions cover the carpet, and an impressive mountain of pillows occupies the middle of the room. A tray holds two steaming mugs of chocolate and enough biscuits to sustain a small military campaign. Molly is wearing a comfortable cream linen nightshirt and loose trousers, her short hair even more unruly than usual.

_Pillows everywhere. A nightshirt. A private room._

Your imagination rallies for one last, rather heroic effort.

"I made us a fort!" Molly announces proudly, pointing at an arrangement of cushions and blankets. "And I found my old favorite pajamas for you. I hope these fit. They're rather large on me, but you are rather large compared with me, so it should work out splendidly."

Oh.

_Oh._

The truth arrives with the slow, terrible majesty of a collapsing cathedral. She means a pajama party. An actual pajama party. With pajamas.

For one brief, shameful moment, you contemplate the distance between the evening you imagined and the evening arranged before you. Then Molly holds up the spare trousers, looking so delighted by her preparations that the disappointment begins to seem rather foolish.

The trousers fit. The top is a little short in the sleeves. Molly considers you for a moment and nods with satisfaction.

"Perfect! Now, the first rule of pajama parties is that nobody has to be terribly grown-up. The second rule is that we mustn't spill chocolate on Margaret's carpet. She was _very_ particular about that."

"And the third rule?" you ask.

"Oh, there isn't one. I only thought of two." She takes a mug, settles cross-legged among the cushions, and looks up at you expectantly.

You take a biscuit. The chocolate smells wonderful. Against all expectations—and perhaps against your better judgment—you find yourself smiling.

parameters.text:
You pick up a pillow and examine it thoughtfully. "And what, exactly, are the rules concerning armed conflict?"

Molly's eyes widen. "Oh, no, you don't—"

Your first strike catches her harmlessly on the shoulder. She retaliates immediately, and with such enthusiasm that you are forced into a strategic retreat behind an armchair. For several glorious minutes, the Royal Pigeon becomes the scene of a battle that military historians will never be permitted to study.

At last Molly collapses onto the cushions, breathless with laughter. "Truce! Truce! I surrender!"

There is a soft knock at the door.

"Miss Moreno?" comes Margaret's impeccably controlled voice. "Is everything quite all right?"

You and Molly look at each other. A feather floats slowly between you.

"Perfectly!" Molly calls. "We're being very quiet!"

The silence on the other side of the door is eloquent. Then Margaret's footsteps retreat down the corridor.

Molly presses a pillow over her mouth to smother another fit of giggles. A moment later you're laughing too, with no trace left of the elaborate evening your imagination had prepared. This is, rather inconveniently, much more fun.

Molly lowers her voice conspiratorially. "I've been trying not to laugh whenever I see Margaret. Do you remember her face when she heard us with the pillows?" She pauses. "Well, we didn't actually see her face, did we? I think that's what makes it worse."

optionTemplates.text: Settle in for chocolate and stories

parameters.text:
You accept a mug and settle beside Molly among the cushions. "I think I'd rather begin with the chocolate. You promised something magnificent."

"And you shall have it!" She offers you the biscuit tin with great ceremony. "My grandmother used to make hot chocolate for all the cousins during winter visits. We would stay up telling stories until someone fell asleep in the middle of one. Usually me."

She recounts a childhood expedition to rescue a kitten from an apple tree, which apparently ended with three children, one confused gardener, and a ladder stuck in a pond. You contribute a story of your own. Molly listens with the rapt attention of someone for whom another person's adventures are as exciting as her own.

After a while she draws her knees up beneath her nightshirt and smiles into her mug. "It's nice, isn't it? Just being silly and comfortable with someone. No lessons, no examinations, nobody expecting us to accomplish anything important."

For once, neither of you feels obliged to improve the evening by doing anything at all. Whatever you thought you were coming here for, you discover that a mug of excellent chocolate and Molly's delighted company are very difficult to improve upon.

"I keep thinking about our pajama evening," Molly says warmly. "The stories, the chocolate... It was lovely to have someone to be completely silly with. Or completely lazy. Both are terribly important skills, I think."

the_party.title: Pillows and Chocolate

text:
Molly finds you just as you are contemplating the rare and precious luxury of a morning without lectures.

"Antonio! You're free today, aren't you? Wonderful! There's a lake in the hills above town. It's beautiful, and hardly anyone ever goes there. We could walk up, have a picnic, and go swimming!"

This is less an invitation than a small avalanche of enthusiasm. Before you've had time to decide how ambitious you feel, Molly produces an enormous picnic basket from behind her back.

"I made sandwiches! And there are apples, cheese, honey cakes... Oh, and towels. Don't worry about carrying it all, I'm quite used to hiking."

So much for a restful morning. Still, the prospect of spending a sunny day with Molly has its attractions. You agree, and she leads you out of town at a brisk pace, chattering about birds, wildflowers, and a fox she once spent three days trying to befriend. The fox, by her account, remained disappointingly committed to being a fox.

An hour later, the path opens onto a little mountain lake, clear and blue beneath a ring of green slopes. Sunlight dances on the water. A willow leans over the shore, and a grassy bank offers an ideal place for the picnic. There isn't another soul in sight.

Molly drops the basket and surveys the scene with satisfaction. "Perfect! I told you it was worth the walk."

She sets aside her walking clothes, revealing simple, opaque linen underclothes: a cream sleeveless top and loose dark-green shorts, both thoroughly practical for swimming. She seems no more self-conscious about this than she would about removing a raincoat. You, on the other hand, have suddenly become very interested in the local geology.

"Coming in?" she asks, stepping toward the water. "It's lovely once you get used to it!"

An inviting lake, a beautiful day, and Molly smiling at you over her shoulder. There are worse ways to spend a weekend.

parameters.text:
You shed your outer clothes, keeping your own modest swimming underclothes, and head for the water. "Last one in has to carry the basket home!"

"Oh, that's not fair!" Molly cries, already running. "You've got a head start!"

She overtakes you before your feet touch the shallows. The first plunge is shockingly cold; your breath vanishes, along with several of your more dignified intentions. Molly surfaces beside you, laughing, and flicks a handful of water in your direction.

You retaliate. A spirited exchange follows, interrupted by a swim toward a sun-warmed rock on the far shore. Molly moves through the water as easily as she does over land, but she slows so you can enjoy the crossing together.

By the time you return, you're pleasantly exhausted. Molly wraps herself in a towel and passes you a honey cake. "That was wonderful! We ought to come here more often."

You consider the long walk home. Then the cake. On balance, she makes a persuasive argument.
Molly's eyes brighten. "Do you remember our race into the lake? I still say you started early!" She laughs. "Not that it helped you very much. We should go back when the weather's lovely."

"I think I'll stay here for a while. Someone ought to defend the picnic from marauding wildlife."

Molly considers this. "A very important responsibility. Especially where honey cakes are concerned."

She goes for a swim while you settle beneath the willow. Watching her splash happily in the blue water, you find that doing absolutely nothing is an occupation with considerable merit.

When Molly returns, she stretches out on a towel beside you and opens the basket. Between mouthfuls of bread and cheese, she points out plants growing along the bank: a cooling herb useful for minor burns, soft moss prized by green artificers, and a little blue flower whose name she can't quite remember.

"I'm not very good at remembering the scholarly names," she admits. "But I know what grows where. My old gardener taught me when I was small."

Together you collect a few useful specimens without disturbing the rest. The afternoon passes in easy conversation, occasional comfortable silences, and one determined attempt by a duck to negotiate a share of the sandwiches. Molly insists that the duck is being perfectly polite.

parameters.title: Wild plants
parameters.description: Molly has extensive practical knowledge of wild plants, learned during her childhood outdoors.

parameters.text: "I found another place that reminds me of our picnic," Molly tells you. "Quiet water, trees, absolutely no one demanding that we study." She thinks for a moment. "Well, there was that duck. But he only demanded sandwiches."

optionTemplates.text: Find out what Molly has in mind

parameters.text: You follow Molly toward the shallows. Something about her smile suggests she's enjoying this invitation for reasons that may have very little to do with swimming.

title: The Lake Above Town

molly_lake_fun.text:
Molly wades in enthusiastically, swims several yards, and turns to wave.

"Come on! Don't be shy!"

You're beginning to suspect that Molly is considerably less shy than she sometimes appears. Well, there's only one thing for it. You leave your shirt and trousers on the bank, keeping your modest swimming underclothes, and try to ignore the enormous grin with which Molly observes your preparations.

You join her in the water. Almost immediately, a small complication presents itself. Molly's practical linen swimming top, perfectly modest on dry land, has become rather less discreet now that it's soaked. Apparently, the lake has very strong opinions about the laws of transparency.

You're doing your best to behave like a civilized scholar when Molly notices that the view has had a noticeable effect on your composure. Her eyes widen for a heartbeat. Then she breaks into a delighted, wicked little smile.

"Well, Antonio! It seems I'm not the only one who knows how to cast Giant Growth. And I thought you only used that card in _Hordes_!"

There are moments when a rigorous education in magical theory is of absolutely no assistance whatsoever.

Molly glides closer, still smiling. "If you'd like," she adds, lowering her voice, "I could try reversing the effect."

_Gulp._

parameters.text:
You return Molly's smile and draw her gently closer. That, apparently, is all the encouragement she needs.

There follows a considerable amount of splashing, fresh evidence of Molly's formidable wrestling skills, and the abrupt departure of several scandalized birds. The rest is a private matter between two consenting scholars, and the local wildlife has already heard quite enough.

When you finally gather your thoughts, you're standing in the shallows with Molly close against you, her legs wrapped securely around your waist. Both of you are breathless; Molly looks positively radiant.

"Antonio," she whispers into your ear, "we can do that again whenever you like. With or without the water."

She laughs and kisses you. "Just for fun, you know? When we both feel like it. No need to decide the rest of our lives over a swim."

You agree. A remarkably sensible arrangement, considering the astonishing lack of sensible behavior that produced it.

parameters.relationTag: Molly is not as shy as you thought

parameters.text: Molly gives you a mischievous smile. "I've been thinking about that afternoon at the lake. I had no idea swimming could be quite so entertaining." She blushes a little. "We really ought to go again sometime."

Emma greets you with a smile of positively dangerous innocence. "Antonio! Molly was telling me about your excursion to the lake. Apparently there was a rather remarkable demonstration of Giant Growth." You open your mouth to object. "Oh, spare me the technical details. I only wish to congratulate you on finally discovering an application of green magic that inspires genuine enthusiasm for your studies." Her raised eyebrow suggests that further objections would merely improve her afternoon.

You return Molly's smile, and she meets you halfway with a delighted kiss.

There follows a considerable amount of splashing, further evidence of Molly's remarkable wrestling skills, and the abrupt evacuation of several nearby birds. The problem is resolved right there in the lake. Promptly. Perhaps a little _too_ promptly.

Back on the bank, Molly spreads her damp things over a sun-warmed stone. She catches your sheepish expression and laughs—not unkindly, but with infectious amusement.

"Don't worry, Antonio. My enthusiasm does have a way of being contagious." She leans close and lowers her voice. "Next time..." A very knowing smile. "...I'm sure you'll take a little more time."

_Next time._ There are encouraging phrases, and then there are phrases capable of restoring an entire man's self-confidence.

"If you'd like a next time, that is," Molly adds, suddenly a little shy. "I would. Something just for fun, now and then, without making a grand fuss about it."

You tell her you'd like that too. Molly squeezes your hand, plainly delighted with the arrangement.

parameters.relationTag: Molly is not as shy as you thought

parameters.text: Molly smiles and gives your hand a squeeze. "Do you remember our afternoon at the lake? It was lovely, Antonio." Her expression turns impish. "And next time, perhaps we won't be in quite such a hurry."

Emma greets you with a smile of positively dangerous innocence. "Antonio! Molly was telling me about your excursion to the lake. Apparently there was a rather remarkable demonstration of Giant Growth." You open your mouth to object. "Oh, spare me the technical details. I only wish to congratulate you on finally discovering an application of green magic that inspires genuine enthusiasm for your studies." Her raised eyebrow suggests that further objections would merely improve her afternoon.

Oh, dear. That wasn't a bluff.

A strategic withdrawal is clearly in order. Red as a tomato, you begin edging toward the shore, doing your best to conceal the source of Molly's rapidly growing amusement.

"It's just that... you know, reflections in water can create rather misleading impressions of submerged objects..."

Molly nods with exaggerated seriousness. "Oh, yes! Professor Lombard was explaining that in class the other day."

For one glorious moment, you think you've been saved by academic rigor.

"That must be it, of course," she continues solemnly. "Still, I'll be sure to record the results of our experiment."

She bursts into laughter. You cannot help joining in, even as you retreat to the towels with what little dignity remains. Molly follows, cheerful as ever, and offers you a honey cake as a peace treaty.

Molly covers a smile with her hand. "You know, Antonio, I've been thinking about Professor Lombard's lesson on refraction. Such a fascinating subject!" Her eyes sparkle. "We really should repeat our little experiment someday."

Emma studies you with an expression of refined disbelief. "Molly told me about your little swimming expedition. She apparently proposed a most interesting practical experiment, and you fled—citing Professor Lombard's lecture on refraction." She pauses to let this sink in. "Fibonacci, I've always admired a man who knows when to retreat. But to abandon such a promising opportunity in the name of _optics_? Your judgment requires urgent remedial instruction." She looks entirely too pleased with herself.

parameters.title: Not so shy
parameters.description: Molly is definitely not as shy as you thought. If she proposes you some sportive activity, be prepared.

molly_lake_fun.title: A Curious Growth Phenomenon

molly_lake_gift.text:
As you gather the picnic things, Molly suddenly brightens. "Oh! I nearly forgot. I brought you something."

She fishes a green magic card out of a dry pocket in her basket and presents it with a flourish: **Giant Growth**.

{{giftJoke}}

The card is genuinely useful. Molly's pleasure in giving it to you is genuine, too. Her sense of comic timing, however, may be developing into a public menace.
molly_lake_gift.title: A Parting Gift

variants.text: "For your future experiments," she says, with exaggerated scholarly dignity. "In case you decide the optical conditions are more favorable next time."

giftJoke.fallback: "I thought you deserved a souvenir of our afternoon," she says, blushing and smiling at once. "Though judging by what happened earlier, perhaps you didn't need the extra growth after all!"

title: Noble Conduct
text:
You are crossing a side corridor of the Academy when you discover Molly on her knees, scrubbing a stubborn patch of ink from the stone floor. Beside her, two cleaners are moving a heavy bucket between them. Molly's sleeves are rolled to the elbows; she has acquired a streak of soot across one cheek and looks rather pleased with the arrangement.

"Antonio!" She waves the cloth at you. "Did you know the workshop drains clog if you wash powdered iron into them? I didn't! But Marta showed me how to clear one. It's quite clever, really."

"Lady Moreno?"

The voice comes from behind you. Elsa stands in the doorway, immaculately dressed, staring at Molly's wet sleeves. The cleaners straighten at once. Molly looks up with an open smile.

"Oh, hello, Elsa! Would you mind passing me that other rag?"

For a moment, the corridor is very quiet.

"You are the daughter of a duke," Elsa says, keeping her voice controlled. "Students here know that. So do the servants. You cannot simply kneel in the corridor and do their work for them."

"Why not? They had three people to clean the whole workshop, and someone spilled an entire bottle of—"

"Because you represent your family, Molly. If people see a noblewoman working as a scullery maid, they will not say what a generous heart she has. They will say the Morenos have forgotten their station. And the next time you need the staff to follow an instruction, what authority will you have left?"

Molly lowers the rag. "I wasn't giving anyone instructions. I was helping."

"Precisely." Elsa's glance flicks toward the cleaners. "That is the problem."

The words land harder than Elsa seems to expect. Molly blinks rapidly. Her mouth trembles; she tries to answer and cannot. A tear slips down her cheek, making a clean track through the soot. The cleaners look at their shoes. Elsa, suddenly aware of her audience, draws herself a little straighter.

"I don't mean to be cruel," she says, with unfortunate timing. "But someone ought to tell you."

Molly wipes her eyes on her sleeve. "You have. Thank you." Her voice is small, but quite steady by the end. She rises, sets down the cloth, and turns to the cleaners. "Marta, you said the storeroom is short of hands on Thursdays. I can come then, too. If you'll have me."

"Of course, miss," Marta replies softly.

Molly nods. She is still crying a little. Apparently, tears are not preventing her from making appointments.

Elsa looks between them, evidently dismayed that her lecture has produced the exact opposite of its intended effect. You have a moment to intervene.

parameters.title: Criticism and conviction
parameters.description: Criticism can hurt her deeply, even bringing her to tears, but she does not abandon a conviction simply because it is painful to defend. She respects the Academy's workers and volunteers alongside them.

parameters.title: Noble obligations
parameters.description: Elsa believes noble status carries public obligations, including maintaining visible distinctions between those who give orders and those who serve. She worries that disregarding such conventions weakens a family's authority.

optionTemplates.text: Challenge Elsa in front of everyone

parameters.text:
"If a title is so fragile that a bucket of water can ruin it," you tell Elsa, "perhaps the title is the problem."

Elsa turns toward you. "How very easy to say when you have no family name to safeguard."

"You're right," you say. "I've had to earn the respect I get. Perhaps that explains my confusion."

It is not the most diplomatic answer of your academic career. Elsa's eyes narrow. She takes a small purse from her belt and puts several coins into Molly's hand, deliberately, where everyone can see.

"Very well. If we are employing noble daughters as cleaners, we should at least pay them properly. I would hate to be accused of exploiting your generosity."

She departs with the dignified speed of someone who desperately wishes to slam a door but has been denied a suitable door.

Molly stares at the coins. "Oh, that wasn't very kind of her." She glances toward the cleaners. "And it wasn't kind to them, either." Turning to you, she presses the purse into your palm. "Would you hold on to these? You can put them toward something useful. I don't want to keep them."

There is no triumph in her voice. She looks relieved that somebody challenged Elsa, but troubled by how much louder the whole business became.

Molly gives you a rueful smile. "Thank you for defending me when Elsa spoke to me like that. I know you meant well." She hesitates. "Next time, perhaps we could do it without making the cleaners wish the floor would swallow them? They already have enough to deal with."

Elsa regards you coolly. "I remember your little speech about titles and buckets, Fibonacci. A spirited performance. Unfortunately, governing a household requires rather more than spirited performances." A faint, reluctant smile appears. "Though I confess it was a memorable line."

optionTemplates.text: Stay with Molly after Elsa leaves

parameters.text:
You let Elsa go without a reply. Instead, you kneel beside Molly and pick up the abandoned rag.

"I think you missed a spot," you say.

Molly gives a watery laugh. "I think I missed several. My eyes went all blurry. It's terribly inconvenient."

You work together in silence until Marta takes the bucket away. Only then does Molly sit back on her heels. "Elsa probably thinks she's helping me," she says. "Perhaps she is, in her own way. But she made Marta feel ashamed of letting me help. That's the part I can't bear."

"You can still help her," you say. "And you don't have to be cheerful every second of it."

"Thank goodness." Molly sniffs, then brightens. "Because I seem to have used up today's supply."

Later, she finds you with three cards laid out carefully in her hands. "I wanted to give you something for staying. Pick whichever you like! They're all useful, and I promise none of them have ever cleaned a drain."

Molly smiles, a little shyly. "Do you remember when you stayed and helped me finish cleaning after Elsa's lecture? I was having an awful time of it. I don't think I even thanked you properly." She pauses. "Thank you. It meant more than you know."

optionTemplates.text: Ask the workers what would actually help

parameters.text:
"Marta," you ask, "if Molly and I wanted to make this easier next week, what would you need?"

Marta eyes the bucket. "A second handcart would be a start. And a place to sort all the useful bits the workshops throw away. They leave everything mixed with broken glass, and we spend half our time picking through it."

Molly looks up, her tears momentarily forgotten. "They throw away useful materials?"

"Not useful to the professors," Marta says. "Useful to anyone willing to sort them."

You suggest a separate collection bin for metal offcuts and usable scraps. Molly immediately volunteers to speak to the workshop steward and arrange a cart; Marta insists that the staff decide where the bins go. Within a few minutes, the cleaners are explaining their work to two students who are, for once, listening.

When Elsa sees the discussion turning into a practical arrangement, she hesitates by the doorway. "A proper system would at least be preferable to noble students randomly scrubbing floors," she remarks. She considers the bins. "They ought to be labeled."

"That's a good idea!" Molly says earnestly. Elsa seems unsure what to do with the compliment.

A little later, Marta brings you a neatly wrapped bundle. "First things we rescued from the discard basket. You two can have them. Better used than melted down for nothing."

Inside are three small pieces of silver. Astonishing, really, what an institution can overlook when somebody else is expected to sweep it up.

"Marta says the new sorting bins are working!" Molly beams. "It's funny—we meant to help clean the floor, and now they have less to clean in the first place. I wonder what else we've all been doing the difficult way?"

Elsa folds her arms. "That system for collecting workshop scraps? Yes, I heard about it. Sensible enough, once somebody remembered to involve the staff who actually do the work." She gives you a measuring look. "Do try not to look so astonished that I approve of something."

title: A Letter with a Seal
text:
Molly is making her way through an Academy corridor with a basket balanced on one arm and a stack of books pressed against her chest. A loaf of sweet bread protrudes from the basket at a precarious angle. She greets you enthusiastically, which proves too much for the entire arrangement.

One book slides free. Then another. The bread makes a bid for independence. You catch the basket just as a heavy envelope flutters to the floor.

The envelope is thick cream paper, folded with almost military precision and closed by an imposing red wax seal. A coat of arms is pressed into it, surrounded by enough flourishes to suggest that the sender has never written an informal note in their life. Across the front, in impeccable calligraphy, is Molly's name—accompanied by an impressive procession of titles.

"Oh! My letter." Molly snatches up the envelope, then catches herself. "Sorry, Antonio. I didn't mean to grab it from you. Thank you for saving the cakes!"

She slips the letter between her books, but not before you notice the corner is creased from being opened and folded again. Her sunny expression falters for a moment.

"It's from home," she explains. "They want to know how my studies are going. Whether I've made the proper acquaintances. Whether I'm making progress toward... well, the things I'm supposed to do afterward."

She looks down at her basket. "The cakes are for some of the first-years. They looked terribly miserable after the alchemy test. I was going to cheer them up."

Apparently the first-years' spirits are an urgent matter. The weight of a family dynasty is rather less convenient to carry around in a basket.

parameters.title: Expectations from home
parameters.description: Molly's family expects regular reports on her academic progress, social connections, and preparation for responsibilities after the Academy. Their expectations make her uneasy.

parameters.text:
"You don't have to explain," you tell her, handing back the books. "It looks like a private letter."

Molly's shoulders relax. "Thank you. It's not a secret, exactly. It's just... complicated."

She hesitates, studying the seal. "Everyone at home is very certain about what would make me useful. I suppose they're trying to look after me."

You let the subject rest. Molly places the letter safely beneath her books, then offers you a pastry with the solemn gratitude of someone bestowing a medal.

"Here. For rescuing the basket. And for not asking questions I don't quite know how to answer yet."

Molly smiles warmly. "Do you remember that great disaster with my basket and the letter from home? You didn't press me about it, even though I was acting so strangely. That was kind of you, Antonio. I haven't forgotten."

optionTemplates.text: Offer to help with her reply

parameters.text:
"Would it help if we worked on a reply together? Not the private parts. Just the part about your studies."

Molly considers this with immediate relief. "Oh, that would be wonderful! I always get stuck trying to sound... important."

You suggest beginning with what she has actually been doing: lessons attended, exercises completed, people met. Molly counts these on her fingers, then adds, "And I helped some children with their reading! Although I don't suppose that counts as academic progress."

"Why shouldn't it? You've learned enough to teach somebody else."

"Oh! That's true, isn't it?" Her face brightens. "I never thought of putting it that way."

She pulls a little notebook from her basket and begins jotting down ideas. After a moment, she pauses. "I still want to tell them the truth. I'm not getting top marks. And I haven't decided what I want to do afterward."

"Then that's what the letter should say."

"Yes," Molly says, quietly but firmly. "I think it should."

The draft, when she reads it back to you, is less grand than the envelope. It is also unmistakably hers.

"I sent that letter we worked on," Molly tells you. "I was so nervous about being honest that I nearly rewrote it in proper formal language." She smiles. "But I didn't. Thank you for helping me find the words."

You gesture toward the envelope peeking out between her books. "Molly, I had no idea one could fit an entire family history into a blob of wax. Do they send invitations to breakfast by royal proclamation?"

Molly takes the envelope and peers at it seriously. "Well, breakfast invitations are usually on smaller paper."

You look at her. She looks at you. Then she realizes what you mean and starts laughing.

"Oh, Antonio! No, not every breakfast! Only when we have guests." She pauses. "That sounded worse, didn't it?"

"A little."

"I once tried to send my brother a letter with a drawing of a duck instead of a proper seal," she confesses. "The household secretary sent it back because he thought someone had tampered with the correspondence."

You suggest that the duck may have been insufficiently heraldic. Molly laughs so hard she has to put the basket down before the pastries make a second escape.

"I know they're trying to be proper," she says when she catches her breath. "But sometimes I wish they'd just write, 'Dear Molly, how are you?'"

Molly bites back a grin. "I received another letter from home. The seal is enormous, as usual." Her eyes brighten. "I've been thinking about your idea. Perhaps I should ask them to put a duck on it next time. A very dignified duck, of course."

title: Kitchen Volunteers
text:
The smell reaches you before the noise: onions, fresh bread, and something that may once have been soup but is currently reconsidering its place in the world.

You follow the commotion to the Academy cafeteria kitchen. A cook is trying to rescue a boiling pot, an assistant is counting plates with the expression of a defeated general, and Molly stands in the middle of it all wearing an enormous borrowed apron. Her cheeks are flushed, her sleeves rolled up, and three vegetables are balanced precariously against her elbow.

"Antonio! Thank goodness!" she cries. One of the vegetables escapes. "I only came to help with lunch. They were short-handed, and I thought, how difficult can chopping and stirring be?"

There are many possible answers. The state of the kitchen suggests she has been discovering them experimentally.

{{referral}}

Molly points to the great pot. "I followed the recipe! Well, most of it. I was trying to make enough for everyone, so I multiplied everything by four. Including the salt." She lowers her voice. "And perhaps the pepper."

The head cook, a broad-shouldered woman with flour on both forearms, looks you over. "If you're here to help, pick a station. If you're here to admire the disaster, take a number."

Molly clasps her hands hopefully. "Oh, Antonio, will you? I really do want to be useful."

variants.text:
Emma is leaning against the doorframe, having evidently delivered you to the scene with the air of a scholar unveiling an important discovery. "I recommended you," she announces. "After tasting Antonio's cooking, I thought you deserved competent assistance. Also, if I have to eat what is currently in that pot, I intend to hold somebody accountable."

"Emma!" Molly looks scandalized. "It isn't _that_ bad."

Emma samples one cautious spoonful. Her face remains admirably composed. "No. Quite right. The salt is excellent. One can almost detect a soup underneath it."

Molly looks at you helplessly as Emma retreats toward lunch, her good deed apparently complete.

referral.fallback: "One of the staff told me you've worked in a proper kitchen," Molly explains. "I hope you don't mind that I asked them about you. I wasn't spying! I just thought you might know how to save lunch." She surveys the pots and gives you an apologetic smile. "You could say it's a little urgent."

parameters.title: Eager but inexperienced
parameters.description: Molly readily volunteers for practical work, but enthusiasm sometimes outruns her knowledge. She can admit mistakes and is keen to learn rather than leave the work to others.

optionTemplates.text: Teach Molly a recipe she can make again

parameters.text:
"First," you say, gently removing a knife from beneath a precarious pile of carrots, "let's make something simple. Something that won't require an emergency committee."

Molly nods with deep seriousness. "Excellent. An emergency committee sounds terribly time-consuming."

You show her how to prepare a sturdy vegetable stew: brown the onions, cut the vegetables to similar sizes, add stock gradually, taste before seasoning, and keep the heat low. Molly follows your hands carefully and asks questions—not always the expected ones. "How do you know when an onion is properly browned?" is followed by "Do onions mind being browned?" The latter requires a moment of reflection from everyone involved.

When the stew is ready, the head cook tastes it and nods. "Good. And she made most of that herself."

Molly positively glows. "I did! Well, Antonio stopped me from adding four times the salt again, but otherwise I did!"

After the meal, the cook presents you with a compact, well-kept kit of utensils and measuring implements. "We have a spare. A cook who teaches instead of shouting can put it to use."

Molly takes your hand in both of hers. "Next time, perhaps I can cook something for you. Something edible, I mean."

parameters.name: Cooking set
parameters.description: A compact, well-kept kit of utensils and measuring implements.

parameters.text: Molly beams when you mention cooking. "I've been practicing the stew you taught me! I even remembered to taste it before adding salt." She lowers her voice conspiratorially. "The cook says that's the first principle of not poisoning an entire dining hall."

You take stock of the room. There are six cooks, three chopping boards, enough potatoes to provision an army, and no clear idea who is doing what. The ingredients are fine. The arrangement is a catastrophe wearing an apron.

"Molly, take charge of washing and sorting the vegetables. Ask the cooks what they need first. I'll clear the worktops and set up stations."

"Me? Take charge?" She looks alarmed, then glances at the exhausted assistants. "All right! Everyone, please tell me what you need. One at a time—oh! Sorry, I was shouting too."

You separate preparation from cooking, move the flour away from the washbasin, and get the assistants working in a sensible order. Molly turns out to have a gift for remembering whose hands are full and who has been waiting too long for help. Once the work has a rhythm, she keeps it going with cheerful, practical attention.

By lunchtime the dishes arrive hot, the plates arrive clean, and the kitchen is quiet enough to hear the head cook mutter in disbelief.

"I was going to send these back to the workshop," she says, handing you three unused moxes from a box of surplus kitchen requisitions. "They'll do more good in an artificer's hands. Consider them thanks for saving the service."

Molly looks at the tidy counters, pleased but thoughtful. "I wanted to do everything myself. It turns out asking everyone what they need works rather better."

"I tried your kitchen trick again," Molly tells you proudly. "I asked everyone what they needed before doing anything. It worked wonderfully!" She hesitates. "I did still burn the onions. But nobody had to wait for a plate."

You notice a small rack of culinary artificery cards beside the stove: common green-essence tools for preserving herbs, coaxing vegetables to ripen, and keeping produce fresh on long journeys. Molly catches your glance and immediately brightens.

"Oh! We could use those! Do you think one could fix the soup?"

"The soup has made its choices," you say. "Let's start with the vegetables."

You select a harmless growth-aspected card and carefully adjust its application to a tray of wilted herbs. Under the cook's watchful eye, the leaves straighten, turn fresh green, and release a vivid fragrance. Molly is delighted. She offers suggestions, helps you compare the effects on different leaves, and discovers that a small, controlled influence produces much better results than the enthusiastic overuse she initially proposes.

The cook adds the revived herbs to a new pot. This time, when she tastes the result, her eyebrows rise in genuine approval.

"There," Molly says, looking from the herbs to the card in your hand. "I've never understood green essence so well in class. Apparently I needed it explained by a parsley leaf."

You find yourself understanding its practical behavior more clearly, too. A lesson learned over a boiling pot is still a lesson—even if nobody will award you a scholarly medal for it.

Molly smiles at you. "I used that green-essence trick on some herbs again! Very carefully, just as you showed me." She pauses. "The parsley was splendid. The basil was rather enthusiastic. I'm still working on the basil."

title: The Worst Student in the Best Study Group
text:
Molly has commandeered a table in the Academy library and fortified it with books, practice cards, three cups of tea, and a plate of biscuits. She has also recruited Emma and you to help her prepare for the upcoming artificery examination. The biscuits, at least, suggest a sound understanding of the principles of successful collaboration.

"Thank you both so much!" she says as you sit down. "I really have been studying, but everything becomes muddled when the professors ask me to explain it. I thought perhaps if we worked together..."

"Naturally," Emma replies. She draws a neat diagram in Molly's notebook. "The central distinction is between essence affinity and the allocation of a card's expressive capacity. Once you've accounted for the constraints on manifestation, the rest follows."

Molly considers this in silence. "Yes," she says brightly. "Of course."

Emma advances to a second diagram. It has more arrows. "Now, in the case of a composite effect—"

"Sorry," Molly interrupts softly. "Could we perhaps go back to the first arrow?"

Emma looks down at her page. "Which first arrow?"

"The one before all the other arrows."

You watch Emma take a slow breath. For a young woman capable of explaining a complex enchantment in four elegant sentences, the discovery that four sentences might not be enough is proving unexpectedly educational.

Molly notices, too. Her smile thins. "I'm sorry. You're both being so patient. I think I must be the worst student in the best study group at the Academy."

"That's not what I—" Emma begins, then stops. Her expression softens. "Molly, I know you're trying."

"I know." Molly looks at her notes. "I just wish trying felt a little more like understanding."

Emma sets down her pen. The three of you have an evening, a pile of practice cards, and rather more work to do than the biscuits were prepared for. You can approach the problem in several ways.

parameters.title: Academic insecurity
parameters.description: Molly studies seriously but struggles with abstract artificery explanations and compares herself unfavorably to brilliant classmates. This does not reflect a lack of curiosity or practical intelligence.

parameters.text:
"All right," you say, putting Emma's diagram aside. "Forget expressive capacity for a moment. Imagine you're growing a garden."

"Oh!" Molly sits up. "I can imagine that."

You use seeds to represent captured essences, garden beds to represent a card's limited capacity, and different plants to show how the same resources produce different results depending on their arrangement. Molly begins asking questions without apologizing first. Soon she is correcting one of your examples: "But those two plants won't grow happily together. They compete for the same soil. Wouldn't that be like putting incompatible effects on one card?"

Emma blinks. "Actually, yes. Precisely."

"Oh." Molly looks delighted and astonished in equal measure. "I understood one!"

"More than one," you point out. "You just explained the next problem."

By the end of the session Molly has drawn a garden across half a notebook. Its flowers are annotated with surprisingly accurate artificery principles. Emma studies the page and admits, with graceful reluctance, that the method is effective.

As you gather your things, Molly presses two small moxes into your hand. "These were spare practice materials. I think you'll make better use of them than I would tonight. And I'd like to thank you for finding a way to explain things that made sense to me."

Molly greets you with an eager smile. "I used your garden explanation in class! The professor said it was an unconventional comparison, but a very sound one." She pauses. "I didn't tell him the cabbage was your idea. I hope you don't mind."

optionTemplates.text: Practice the game, one decision at a time

parameters.text:
You clear the diagrams away and deal a small practice hand. "Let's forget the examination wording. You've got these cards, this much mana, and an opponent about to attack. What's your move?"

Molly relaxes visibly. "Oh, I know this one. I think."

The first round goes badly. Molly spends her resources too early and leaves her best defender exposed. You reset the position and ask what she would change. On the second attempt she keeps a card in reserve. On the third she spots an unfavorable trade before Emma can point it out.

Emma leans forward, interested despite herself. "Good. Now suppose your opponent is bluffing. What information do you actually have?"

"Not enough," Molly says after a moment. "So I shouldn't bet everything on being right."

Emma smiles. "Exactly."

You work through a dozen little encounters, each illustrating one principle. Emma gradually abandons her prepared lecture and begins inventing increasingly devious positions for Molly to solve. The two of them are laughing by the time Molly wins a practice exchange with a move neither of you suggested.

"There!" Molly announces, triumphantly placing her final card. "I did it myself!"

"And made the correct choice for the correct reason," Emma replies. She turns to you. "A much better teaching method than another hour of definitions, Fibonacci. Nicely judged."

High praise from Emma. You resist the temptation to have the words engraved on a plaque.

Molly grins when the subject of cards comes up. "Remember when you and Emma made me play the same little situations over and over? I actually see the mistakes coming now. Not always in time, but much more often! Emma says that's progress."

optionTemplates.text: Show Molly what she's already good at

parameters.text:
You look at the scattered cards. One of them depicts a creature of the forest; Molly has absentmindedly placed it beside a green incantation and arranged the pair so their effects complement one another.

"Molly," you say, "I've noticed something. Whenever a lesson involves plants, animals, or growth, you stop worrying about the terminology and start seeing how everything connects. You've got a real knack for green essence."

She looks up sharply. "Me?"

"Yes, you. You know what makes living things thrive. You notice details the rest of us miss. That's exactly what this kind of artificery needs."

Molly stares at you. She opens her mouth, closes it, and looks down at the cards again. "I've spent so much time trying to be as good at everything as Emma," she says quietly. "I didn't think there was something I might be particularly good at myself."

Emma reaches for the cards and examines Molly's arrangement. "Antonio is right. I wouldn't have chosen that combination, but it's coherent—and rather clever. I may have been teaching you the subject I find easiest instead of the part that suits you."

"You really think so?" Molly asks.

"I do," Emma says. "Try explaining _your_ choice to us."

And Molly does. Hesitantly at first, then with the eager confidence she brings to a conversation about a new trail or an injured animal. She shows you how the growth effects support the creature rather than simply making it stronger. Following her reasoning, you notice a connection in green artificery that you had previously overlooked.

When she finishes, Molly gives you a long, grateful look. "Antonio... thank you. You made me feel as though I might actually belong here."

For once, her smile is almost shy. Emma quietly pushes the plate of biscuits toward the middle of the table, allowing the moment to remain Molly's.

parameters.title: Affinity for green artificery
parameters.description: Molly has an intuitive grasp of growth, plants, animals, and the relationships between living things. Recognizing this gives her a more confident starting point for her studies.

parameters.text: Molly smiles warmly when she sees you. "I've been studying more green artificery since our evening in the library. I still find some of it terribly difficult, but I don't feel quite so hopeless now." She hesitates. "I keep remembering what you said—that I have a knack for it. It meant a lot to me, Antonio."

text:
Professor Glützenbaum greets the class with his usual enthusiasm, standing behind a desk laden with enchanted cards, pigments, and an alarming assortment of delicate brass instruments.

"Good afternoon, my promising young artificers! This morning, you learned to create. This afternoon, you shall learn to improve! Or, occasionally, to make things worse in a carefully calculated and academically respectable manner."

He holds up a card depicting an armored knight.

"Augmentation! We strengthen an existing enchantment, making our creation more powerful, more resilient, or more capable. Naturally, greater power demands greater magical energy. A stronger card will generally cost more mana to play."

He sets it down and picks up another.

"Distillation! The opposite principle. We remove something from an enchantment, reducing its power but also its cost. A modest creation, efficiently designed, may prove far more useful than an extravagant masterpiece."

"Rather like certain students," someone murmurs from the back.

"Who said that?"

The sharp voice comes from a young man a few seats away. Dark-eyed, handsome, and visibly indignant, he has turned toward his neighbor, who looks utterly bewildered.

"You were looking at me."

"I was looking at the professor!"

"With that expression?"

"What expression?"

"That one!"

Professor Glützenbaum clears his throat.

"Mr. Farid, I presume? An excellent demonstration of excessive energy expenditure. Perhaps we should attempt a little distillation."

The classroom erupts in laughter. Farid's expression darkens, but he eventually folds his arms and settles back into his seat, muttering something about disrespectful northerners.

Glützenbaum returns to his cards, entirely untroubled.

"Now then! You have cards, you have tools, and you have two splendid ways to improve your decks—or ruin them beyond recognition. I suggest you begin with the former."

parameters.title: Proud and quarrelsome
parameters.description: Farid is a young student from an Arabic realm, quick to take offense and fiercely protective of his dignity. He has a fiery temperament and appears entirely willing to argue over the smallest perceived slight.

text:
Professor Glützenbaum enters the classroom carrying a large orange squash under one arm and a stack of papers under the other. He sets the squash on his lectern. It immediately rolls off, hits the floor with a magnificent thud, and continues toward the front row.

"A pumpkin," the professor announces, retrieving it with what dignity remains. "A traditional seasonal decoration. Not, as Mr. Ousmane has suggested, a new examination instrument."

Ousmane looks faintly disappointed.

"Next Saturday evening, the Academy will hold its annual Halloween celebration in the cafeteria. There will be refreshments, music, costumes, and absolutely no unauthorized conjurations. Last year's incident with the animated skeleton has still not been satisfactorily explained."

At the back of the room, Farid quietly puts something away in his bag.

"Attendance is voluntary," Glützenbaum continues. "Costumes are encouraged. Any student attempting to frighten the faculty into cancelling Monday's lessons will receive a failing grade in initiative."

The room erupts into excited conversation. Molly is already smiling; Emma looks thoughtful, as though evaluating the evening's potential benefits against several hours of lost study. You, meanwhile, have a decision to make. Parties are perfectly enjoyable alone. Then again, there are certain people whose company might improve the occasion considerably.

parameters.text:
You decide to keep your options open. An evening of food, music, and watching your classmates make fools of themselves sounds perfectly agreeable without any elaborate arrangements.

Besides, you have an entire week to devise a costume. Surely that is enough time to produce something respectable. Or at least something recognizable.

You catch Emma as the class disperses.

"Emma? About Saturday's party..."

She stops, regarding you with an attentive little smile. "Yes, Antonio?"

You find Molly gathering her books, still looking delighted by the announcement.

"Molly, would you like to go to the party together?"

Her face brightens at once.

title: An Invitation to Fright

parameters.text:
You agree to meet Emma at the cafeteria entrance. She departs with a quick wave, leaving you to contemplate the considerable challenge of finding a costume that won't invite an entire evening of criticism.

An impossible task, perhaps. But not an unpleasant one.

invite_emma.title: A rather interesting proposal

variants.text:
You had a perfectly reasonable sentence prepared. It appears to have deserted you.

"I was wondering if you might... Saturday, that is... the party. With me. If you..."

Emma watches you with growing delight. "Fibonacci, are you inviting me to a party, or attempting to cast a spell without the necessary incantation?"

"The party. Definitely the party."

"How fortunate. I was beginning to worry about your health." She smiles. "Yes, Antonio. I'd be delighted."

"Would you care to go together?" you ask.

Emma's smile turns mischievous. "Another evening of dancing, Antonio? After our last ball, I'm beginning to suspect you've developed a taste for it."

"Would that be a problem?"

"Not in the slightest. But I shall expect you to remember at least some of the steps." She gives you a warm smile. "I'd love to."

"Would you like to go together?"

For once, Emma doesn't seem interested in making you work for an answer. "Yes," she says, smiling. "I was hoping you'd ask."

She seems to realize how readily she's admitted it, and adds, "After all, someone must ensure you don't arrive dressed as an unconvincing turnip."

emmaInvitation.fallback:
"Would you like to go together?" you ask.

Emma considers you for a moment. "A whole evening without studying, competing, or arguing about card mechanics? How very irresponsible of you, Fibonacci."

"Is that a yes?"

"Of course it is." Her mouth curves into a smile. "I wouldn't miss the opportunity to see what you consider a suitable costume."

invite_molly.text:
"Oh! Yes, absolutely!" Molly answers, rather more loudly than she intended. She glances around and laughs. "Sorry. I was just hoping I'd have someone to go with."

"Have you decided on a costume?"

"I've got an idea." She grins, suddenly looking rather pleased with herself. "But I'm not telling you. It's a surprise."

"Should I be frightened?"

"Terribly," she says, in a voice so cheerful that the threat loses most of its force.

She gathers her things, then turns back. "And Antonio? I'm really glad you asked."

parameters.text:
You promise to meet Molly at the cafeteria entrance. She hurries away, already discussing costume ideas with another student.

You have the distinct impression she's going to enjoy this evening enormously. You find yourself looking forward to it too.

invite_molly.title: A delighted acceptance

text:
For one evening, the Academy cafeteria has been transformed beyond recognition. Paper bats hang from the rafters, carved pumpkins grin from every windowsill, and strings of little enchanted lights drift lazily above the tables. Someone has pushed the benches aside to make room for dancing. The kitchen staff, apparently delighted to have an excuse to abandon their usual menu, have prepared enough pastries to sustain a small siege.

A tall figure in a black cloak stands beside the refreshments, inspecting a bowl of punch with professional suspicion. It takes you a moment to recognize Professor Glützenbaum.

"Fibonacci," he says. "Welcome. I am a vampire."

"Very convincing, Professor."

"Thank you. I have been assured that the costume is historically accurate. Do not drink the purple punch. I am told it contains an alarming quantity of sugar."

He takes a generous glass of it himself.

{{ arrival }}

parameters.text:
"Terrifying," you assure her. "I nearly fled."

"How disappointing. I was hoping for actual screaming." Emma offers you her arm. "Come along. I believe the professor is about to discover what happens when one drinks four glasses of punch in quick succession."

"Absolutely terrifying," you say.

Molly beams. "Good! Though I think the tail makes it a little difficult to look menacing."

She takes your hand and draws you into the room before you can offer a more detailed assessment.
You make for the food, where a plate of suspiciously lifelike marzipan fingers has attracted a small crowd. If this is what the Academy calls terror, you are prepared to face it bravely.

title: A Night of Masks

variants.text:
Near the entrance, Emma is waiting for you, dressed as an elegant vampire in a dark, perfectly tailored gown, her pale makeup and neatly pinned hair lending her an almost aristocratic severity. The effect is striking. Her expression, however, is unmistakably Emma's.

"Well, Fibonacci?" She spreads her hands slightly. "Am I sufficiently dreadful?"

Molly appears beside the doorway wearing a wonderfully elaborate werewolf costume, complete with furry ears, a bushy tail, and a pair of padded paws. She gives a fierce little growl, then immediately bursts out laughing.

"Sorry! I've been practicing that all afternoon. Was it scary?"

arrival.fallback: You arrive without a companion, but hardly unnoticed. Ousmane, dressed as a pirate of remarkable elegance, greets you with a sweeping bow. Farid has come as a masked highwayman, a costume that appears to require suspiciously little preparation. They wave you toward the refreshments.

emma_halloween_party.text:
Emma proves an excellent companion for an evening of mild chaos. She informs Professor Glützenbaum that his vampire disguise is undermined by the crumbs in his beard. He replies that these are _historically accurate_ crumbs.

You catch Emma examining the punch, one delicate eyebrow raised. "Do you suppose the professor has realized we're both vampires? I'm afraid the Academy's supply of victims is rather limited."

An answer springs to mind. It involves vampires, sucking, and Emma. It is, by every reasonable measure, an appalling idea.

_No,_ advises the small, overworked part of your brain responsible for preserving your dignity. _Don't say it. Whatever you're thinking, don't._

Unfortunately, the rest of your brain has already begun constructing the sentence.

parameters.text: You summon every scrap of intellect at your disposal in a desperate attempt to keep your mouth shut.
You summon every scrap of intellect at your disposal in a desperate attempt to keep your mouth shut.

emma_halloween_party.title: A dance with a vampire

emma_cuts_you_off.text:
Emma watches your expression change. Her eyes narrow behind her glasses.

"No."

You haven't said anything yet.

"I can see the joke forming, Antonio. You have exactly the face of a man about to say something about vampires sucking." She holds up one finger. "And before you ask: yes, I thought of it first. No, you may not hear my version. It was better."

You open your mouth to protest. She raises a second finger.

"Careful. That would be your second mistake, and it's still early."

The narrator would like to congratulate Emma on averting a catastrophe. The narrator would also like to point out that you were only _considering_ a catastrophe.

Before you can defend yourself, Emma spots Molly across the room, happily passing pastries to a pair of nervous first-year students. An unmistakable gleam appears in Emma's eyes.

"Now," she says, drawing herself up to her full aristocratic vampire height, "watch a professional."

parameters.text: You follow at a discreet distance, eager to see whether Emma's confidence is justified.

emma_cuts_you_off.title: An excellent prevention

emma_scares_molly.text:
Emma approaches Molly from behind, gliding silently between the tables. She bares her little costume fangs and whispers into Molly's ear, in her most dreadful voice, "Beware, mortal. Your blood is mine."

Molly turns around. "Emma! You look _wonderful!"

Before Emma can retreat, Molly wraps her in an enormous werewolf hug. Emma's elegant cape gets trapped under a furry paw, and her carefully arranged collar folds over one ear.

"Molly," comes a muffled voice, "this is not how the encounter is supposed to work."

"Oh! Sorry!" Molly loosens her grip. "Was I meant to be frightened? Shall we try again?"

"Absolutely not." Emma straightens her collar with the dignity of a deposed monarch. "My reputation has suffered enough."

Molly grins, pats Emma's shoulder, and goes back to distributing pastries. Emma watches her leave.

"There's no reasoning with werewolves," she mutters. "They're all teeth and unconditional affection."

The musicians strike up a lively dance, offering Emma a convenient escape from further humiliation. She turns to you and extends a hand.

"Come on, Fibonacci. Perhaps I can salvage this evening by defeating you at something civilized."

parameters.text:
You take her hand. "Is dancing really a competition?"

"Not ordinarily," Emma says. "But you've met me."

emma_scares_molly.title: A fearsome predator

emma_dance.text:
{{ emmaDance }}

You join the dancers. Emma moves with practiced grace, although tonight she seems more interested in having fun than in getting every step right. When you nearly collide with a student dressed as an enormous mushroom, she pulls you aside at the last instant—and laughs hard enough to miss a step herself.

"Not a word, Fibonacci. Nobody saw that."

"The mushroom saw."

"The mushroom knows what's good for him."

parameters.text:
"You know, I don't think I've ever seen you laugh quite so much."

"That's because you're usually too busy giving me reasons to sigh." Emma considers this, then smiles. "But perhaps I've been taking myself a little too seriously. Don't tell anyone. I have an image to maintain."

She squeezes your hand briefly as the music carries you both back into the crowd.

optionTemplates.text: Challenge her to one more dance

parameters.text:
"One more? Unless you're afraid I might outdance you."

Emma looks delighted. "There it is. The brave confidence of a man who has learned absolutely nothing."

She takes your hand and leads you straight back onto the floor. You suspect you've just committed yourself to a very long evening.

emma_dance.title: The vampire waltz

variants.text: "You remember our last dance, don't you?" she asks. "I've decided to measure your progress. I may even publish the results. Anonymously, if they're dreadful."

emmaDance.fallback: "Don't look so alarmed," she says. "I promise not to grade your footwork. I left the marking rubric at home."

emma_gift.text:
The party is winding down when Emma draws you aside, away from the music. From a small pocket in her gown she produces a card depicting a bespectacled vampire with a smug little smile. The resemblance is difficult to miss.

"A seasonal experiment," she explains. "Entirely frivolous, academically indefensible, and remarkably effective. I thought you'd appreciate a card with some intelligence behind the fangs."

You glance at the illustration. "You gave yourself glasses."

"Of course. I'm not going to spend eternity squinting."

She places the card in your hand. "And before you ask, it isn't a declaration of undying devotion. That would be terribly on the nose, given the costume."

Her smile softens. "Thank you for inviting me, Antonio. I had a lovely evening. Even if my reign of terror lasted approximately four seconds."
emma_gift.title: A little something

molly_halloween_party.text:
Molly throws herself into the festivities with infectious enthusiasm. She insists you sample the pumpkin pastries, introduces you to half a dozen students you already know, and somehow becomes involved in a contest to see who can make the most convincing monster noise.

Her attempt at a werewolf howl is impressive. Unfortunately, it is immediately followed by a fit of giggles. Ousmane awards her second place, on the grounds that the first-place contestant frightened him more and he refuses to admit it.

Later, the music slows. Molly glances toward the dancers, then back at you. "Would you like to dance? I'm not terribly good at the fancy steps, but I can usually manage not to tread on anyone."

You join the others, moving with considerably more enthusiasm than elegance. Molly laughs when you get the steps wrong and cheerfully admits when she does too. By the end of the song, you're both slightly breathless.

parameters.text:
"You know, I think you make an excellent werewolf."

"Really?" Molly looks delighted. "I spent ages making the ears!"

She wiggles them experimentally, then dissolves into laughter. "All right, perhaps I'm not very frightening. But I'm having a wonderful time."

"Another one?" you ask.

Molly smiles. "I'd love to! Though I should warn you, I get a bit carried away when the music gets faster."

A moment later, the musicians oblige. You discover that this was not an idle warning.

molly_halloween_party.title: The gentlest werewolf

molly_gift.text:
As the last guests begin collecting their cloaks, Molly stops you near the door. "Oh! I nearly forgot. I made something for you."

She produces a card from a little pouch at her waist. Its illustration depicts a cheerful woodland werewolf beneath a bright autumn moon, surrounded by curling green enchantments.

"I thought it would be fun to make a Halloween card," she explains. "And then I thought you might like to have it. It's not as clever as some of the things Emma makes, but I put a lot of care into it."

You turn it over in your hands. The craftsmanship is lovely, and Molly watches your reaction with hopeful anticipation.

When you thank her, she breaks into a radiant smile. "I'm so glad! And thank you for coming with me, Antonio. This was one of the nicest evenings I've had in ages."
molly_gift.title: A handmade surprise

solo_party.text:
Going alone turns out to have its advantages. You are free to wander between conversations, sample the entire pastry selection without negotiation, and observe the costume contest from a strategically safe distance.

Henry's elaborate ghost costume earns enthusiastic applause until he trips over his own sheet. Ousmane declares this a triumph of realism. Farid, meanwhile, wins a special mention for his highwayman costume, largely because nobody can establish whether he's actually wearing a costume at all.

At some point Molly pulls you into a group dance, Emma offers an amused commentary from the sidelines, and Professor Glützenbaum solemnly announces that the evening has been a great success. He is wearing a paper bat on his hat and appears entirely unaware of it.

You leave the cafeteria pleasantly tired, thoroughly fed, and in possession of several memories that should prove useful whenever your classmates become too dignified for their own good.
solo_party.title: A perfectly respectable evening

text: Before enchanting class, the academy sometimes runs a sports hour—mostly laps, and plenty of them. Across the track you spot Emma and Molly jogging side by side, chatting pleasantly as they go. Molly looks thoroughly at ease, sporty and unfazed, while Emma is clearly struggling to keep up, gasping between words as she tries to hold the conversation.

parameters.text: You compliment Molly on her shape. She beams, clearly pleased.
You compliment Emma on her figure. She scoffs—but you catch her smile.
You taunt Emma as you pass them. She smirks.

text:
Well, that's done. First year's tuition paid.

And you're broke again.

Three years of savings, gone in the time it took an administrator to stamp a piece of paper. You'd better pass those exams. Preferably with honors. Preferably without starving in the meantime.

You make your way through the crowded Academy corridor, dodging students, luggage, and an elderly professor who appears to be arguing with his own hat.

That's when you notice her.

A young woman is studying the timetable pinned to the noticeboard. First year, judging by the schedule she's examining. Like you, then.

Unlike you, she seems to know exactly what she's doing.

She turns toward the village, carrying a precarious tower of books that looks as though it might require its own structural engineer.

Naturally, you decide to offer your assistance.

A perfectly chivalrous impulse. One that has absolutely nothing to do with the long, graceful legs visible beneath her skirt.

You catch up and call out to her.

She turns.

Bright green eyes settle on you, appraising you with an intelligence that would probably be intimidating if you were currently capable of rational thought.

You should introduce yourself.

Yes. That would be sensible.

Or perhaps explain why you've stopped her.

Also sensible.

You could even try speaking. People do that, apparently.

"Take your time," she says at last, one eyebrow rising. "It's not as though I'm carrying half the Academy library."

Her expression hovers somewhere between amusement and resignation.

You have the distinct impression that this is not the first time she's had this effect on a young man.

parameters.text:
You clear your throat, summon the scattered remains of your dignity, and manage a smile.

"Sorry. I was going to ask if you needed a hand. Antonio, by the way."

"Emma. A pleasure, Antonio."

She adjusts the stack of books with surprising ease.

"And thank you, but I'm rather stronger than I look."

With a quick wink, she strides away toward the village, leaving you with the uncomfortable suspicion that she has already formed a fairly accurate opinion of you.

optionTemplates.text: A complete failure of higher reasoning

parameters.text:
This is absurd.

You've barely arrived at the Academy, and already you're being subjected to this sort of sorcery. Without warning. On the very first day.

Surely there ought to be regulations.

Nobody should be allowed to have legs like that without some sort of advance notice.

"Emma, by the way," she says, rescuing the conversation from its untimely death. "Delighted to meet you, mysterious stranger."

She sets off at a brisk pace.

A few steps later, she glances back over her shoulder.

"Oh, and one more thing..."

A mischievous smile curls at the corner of her mouth.

"The dark, silent, mysterious type? Doesn't work on me."

And with that, she disappears into the crowd.

You remain where you are for several seconds, contemplating what may well be the most spectacular conversational defeat of your academic career.

"Fibonacci!" Emma greets you with a smile of unmistakable recognition. "I see you've recovered the use of your legs. An encouraging sign." You assure her your legs were never the problem. "Quite right. It was speech that deserted you, wasn't it?" She considers you a moment. "Well, you've managed three whole sentences today. At this rate, we may have a proper conversation before graduation."

title: A Rather Unfortunate First Impression

parameters.title: First impressions
parameters.description: A striking young woman with sharp green eyes, an impressive collection of books, and an equally impressive talent for making you feel foolish. Apparently a fellow first-year student.

manualTrigger: There is a pretty girl over there!

text:
This is a risky move. Perhaps a little too aggressive? Well, fortune favors the bold. According to Henry, Emma Delamain is probably the strongest player at the Academy. After you, naturally.

You commit to the attack.

She doesn't see it coming. Victory!

Across the table, Emma realizes her mistake immediately—but a quarter of a second too late. A flash of anger crosses her delicate, heart-shaped face. Her shoulders sink, and for a brief moment she looks almost wounded. Then she straightens, gathers her composure, and meets your eyes.

"{{greeting}}Well played, Fibonacci."

She glances at the board once more, her brow furrowing. For a moment, she seems to be debating something with herself.

"Tell me. Was that a bluff, or had you calculated it from the beginning?"

parameters.text:
You conceal your considerable satisfaction and begin explaining your reasoning, starting several turns before the decisive attack. Emma listens without interrupting, her eyes moving between you and the cards still scattered across the table.

Then comes a question. A very precise question. You answer it, only to be met with another. Before long, the two of you are reconstructing the entire match, debating alternatives, and examining moves neither of you had considered at the time.

Emma's bitterness gradually disappears, replaced by intense concentration. At one point she even smiles, apparently delighted to have discovered a particularly elegant possibility. Losing, it seems, becomes considerably more tolerable when there is something interesting to learn from it.

Eventually, she rises, a little stiffly, and gathers her belongings. She regards you for a long moment, her expression thoughtful.

"Interesting, Antonio. Very interesting." A faint smile touches her lips. "Until next time."

"I've been thinking about that first match," Emma says. "Not the defeat, naturally. I've recovered from that magnificent tragedy." She traces an imaginary move across the table. "You showed me an alternative I'd completely overlooked. It was infuriatingly elegant." You ask whether this counts as praise. "It counts as an invitation to explain your next trick before you use it on me."

Oh, this is too good. The Academy's brightest star, defeated by Antonio Fibonacci himself! Surely a little celebration is in order.

"Bluff? Me?" You give an extravagant shrug. "My dear Delamain, I was merely trying to give you a sporting chance."

Emma's eyes narrow. For a moment, you wonder whether you've pushed your luck.

"A sporting chance?" she repeats, very slowly.

"Well, I wouldn't want you to lose confidence. You have such a promising future."

Emma stares at you. Then, despite herself, a reluctant smile breaks through.

"How extraordinarily generous of you, Fibonacci. I shall treasure your encouragement."

She begins gathering her cards, then pauses.

"Although I do hope you're prepared for our next match."

"Naturally."

"Good. Because I intend to make you regret every single word of this conversation."

She flashes you a dazzling smile.

"And I shall be insufferably gracious about it."

"Tell me, Fibonacci, are you still generously allowing your opponents a sporting chance?" Emma asks. You suggest that someone must encourage the Academy's promising students. "How charitable." Her smile sharpens. "I have been practicing since our last match. I intend to repay your kindness in full, preferably while you still have enough cards left to appreciate it."

Oh, no. She's waiting for an answer.

This is your chance, Antonio. You've just defeated the most formidable player at the Academy. Surely you can manage a few clever words. Something confident. Something memorable. Something that will make her look at you differently.

You open your mouth.

And then she looks at you with those eyes.

Really, this is most unfair. How is a man supposed to think under such circumstances? You had an entire strategy worked out a moment ago. Where has it gone? Perhaps it's hiding under the table.

"Well, I... that is, the thing about the attack..."

Emma raises an eyebrow. Then recognition dawns, and the corner of her mouth curls upward.

"Ah, yes. My silent admirer. I remember you."

She allows herself a small, thoroughly delighted smile.

"Well, it seems you're rather better at strategy than rhetoric."

She gathers her cards and stands. Her expression softens for a fleeting moment, the teasing smile becoming something almost affectionate.

"Until next time, Antonio."

And with that, she walks away, leaving you with a magnificent victory, a thoroughly ruined speech, and the uncomfortable suspicion that she enjoyed every second of it.

"Antonio, a question," Emma says gravely. "How can a man devise a winning attack involving six cards, then lose the ability to assemble six consecutive words?" You object to this characterization. "Oh, so the ability has returned!" She smiles. "Marvelous. Perhaps next time we play, I'll allow you to choose whether the competition is strategy or conversation."

title: A Worthy Opponent

parameters.title: Competitive nature
parameters.description: Emma takes competition very seriously. She hates losing, but recognizes genuine skill in an opponent and is determined to learn from her mistakes.

variants.text: We met the first day right? Anyways.

text:
You find Emma studying a collection of cards, meticulously arranged across a table. She looks up as you approach.

"Antonio. To what do I owe the pleasure?"

You produce your latest creation, the _Happy Little Accident_, and place it before her.

"Another masterpiece, Fibonacci?" she asks, with a faint smile. "How fortunate that modesty isn't one of your weaknesses."

She picks up the card, apparently intending to give it a cursory inspection. Then she turns it toward the light. Her smile fades into concentration.

"Hmm."

She studies the card more closely, examining the intricate blue enchantments. For a moment, she seems to forget you're there.

"Interesting. Very interesting, actually."

She catches herself, sets the card down, and folds her hands.

"Well. It's certainly not terrible. How did you manage this?"

title: The Ballet Incident
text:
You're enjoying a peaceful break in the cafeteria with Molly, Henry and Ousmane when Elsa bursts in, barely containing her laughter.

"You simply _must_ come and see this! It's hilarious! She thinks she's some sort of fairy!"

The four of you exchange puzzled looks.

"Emma, that insufferable little princess! Oh, just come along!"

Curiosity gets the better of you, and you follow Elsa through the Academy corridors to a small exercise hall.

Inside, Emma is practicing ballet alone. Dressed in a simple dance outfit, she stands beside a wooden barre, one hand resting lightly upon it. Her other hand holds her raised foot high above her head, at the end of a perfectly straight, almost impossibly vertical leg. Her balance is flawless, her expression one of absolute concentration. She hasn't noticed you.

Elsa turns toward the group, positively glowing with anticipation of the sarcastic remarks to come.

Instead, she finds Molly applauding very softly, her face alight with admiration, and three young men standing perfectly still, mouths hanging open, apparently hypnotized.

{{emmaSmittenReaction}}

Elsa's triumphant smile collapses.

"Oh, for heaven's sake! You're all _hopeless!_"

She storms off, her indignant footsteps echoing so loudly through the hall that Emma finally notices her audience.

Henry and Ousmane, caught red-handed, turn scarlet and beat a hasty retreat. Molly gives Emma a delighted smile and an enthusiastic thumbs-up before following them.

And suddenly, there's only you.

Emma calmly lowers her leg, turns toward you, and raises one eyebrow. A mischievous little smile plays at the corner of her mouth, as though she's daring you to say something.

variants.text: Honestly, this girl ought to be illegal. How on earth are you supposed to get any sleep tonight?

emmaSmittenReaction.fallback: You have to admit, it's quite a sight. You'd known Emma was talented, but apparently her determination to excel extends well beyond the card table.

parameters.text:
You incline your head appreciatively.

"I went to see the National Ballet back home last year. I must say, you wouldn't have looked out of place on that stage. Holding a pose like that with such grace isn't something one sees every day."

Emma's raised eyebrow slowly settles.

"Well, Fibonacci. I had no idea you were a patron of the fine arts."

A mischievous smile touches her lips.

"You really ought to invite our dear Baroness sometime. A little culture might do her a world of good."

She gives you a graceful little wave as she heads toward the changing rooms.

No pressure whatsoever."
