Emma relaxes at once, a broad, infectious smile spreading across her face.

"No, I believe she rolled a critical failure on that particular spell."

She glances toward the corridor, still smiling.

"All that effort to assemble an audience, too. Poor Elsa. One almost feels sorry for her."

"Almost?"

"Let's not get carried away, Antonio."

She gives you a conspiratorial wink before collecting her things.

"I wonder whether Elsa has recovered from her great ballet triumph," Emma muses. You ask which triumph she means. "The one where she assembled an audience to ridicule me and accidentally organized a standing ovation." Emma laughs at the memory. "Molly was wonderfully kind. The others looked as though they'd forgotten why they had feet. And Elsa—oh, her face was worth the rehearsal."

"Emma, er... hello. I... very nice, yes. Very straight, and everything..."

Emma approaches with the delighted expression of a cat that has just discovered a particularly entertaining mouse.

"Ah, Antonio! My most devoted admirer! I see you're quite the ballet enthusiast. The tutus, the flexibility, the _physique_, above all. Am I right?"

Oh, dear.

"Er, yes. The physique. Exceptional, yes..."

Emma's smile grows positively wicked.

"Antonio, if we're going to be seeing each other in class all year, you'll really have to learn to resist certain enchantments."

She pauses, looking you straight in the eye.

"Otherwise, I'm afraid your grades are going to suffer terribly."

She walks away with a perfectly innocent expression, leaving you to contemplate the urgent need for remedial lessons in magical resistance.

"Good afternoon, Antonio. How are your studies in magical resistance progressing?" Emma asks sweetly. You hesitate. "Ah. Still struggling, I see." She demonstrates a perfectly ordinary stretch of her shoulder, then regards you with scholarly interest. "Perhaps my ballet rehearsal was simply too advanced for a first-year student. Do let me know when you're ready for the remedial course."

You shrug, doing your best to look unimpressed.

"Not bad, Delamain. A little showy, perhaps."

Emma's eyebrow climbs a little higher.

"Showy?"

"Well, you certainly know how to make an entrance. Or rather, how to keep an audience."

Emma studies you for a moment. Then a slow smile spreads across her face.

"Oh, I see. Everyone else is applauding, so naturally you must be difficult."

She takes a step closer, her eyes sparkling with amusement.

"Tell me, Antonio. Is it that you're genuinely unimpressed, or that you simply can't bear to admit I might be good at something?"

You return her smile.

"Wouldn't want you getting complacent."

Emma laughs.

"How very considerate of you. I'll be sure to return the favor."

She gives you a mockingly gracious little bow before heading toward the changing rooms.

"I practiced a new ballet sequence yesterday," Emma says. "But I'm reluctant to demonstrate it." You ask why. "I fear it might be a little showy." Her expression is perfectly solemn. Then she laughs. "You really did call that performance showy, Antonio. I've decided to treasure the remark. One day I'll find something you're proud of and repay you precisely."

title: League Champion
text:
The applause has barely died down when Emma approaches you, a glass of sparkling wine in hand.

"Well, well. Antonio Fibonacci, league champion. I suppose I'll have to start taking you seriously."

Her teasing smile gives way to something more sincere.

"Congratulations, Antonio. Truly. You've earned this. Winning a match is one thing, but maintaining that level of play throughout an entire season? That's quite an achievement."

She raises her glass in your honor.

parameters.text: "Our reigning league champion," Emma says, raising an imaginary glass. "I suppose I ought to offer my congratulations again." You tell her once was enough. "Nonsense. Winning a whole season deserves recognition." She pauses just long enough to seem sincere. "Enjoy the title, Antonio. I intend to relieve you of its burdens at the earliest opportunity."

"Thank you, Emma. That means a lot, coming from you."

Her expression softens into a warm smile.

"Don't get too sentimental, Fibonacci. I'm still planning to take that title from you next season."

She touches her glass to yours.

"But tonight, it's yours. Enjoy it."

She laughs, shaking her head.

"Enjoy your reign, Fibonacci. I'll be the first to celebrate when it ends."

"Celebrate?"

She raises her glass again, her eyes sparkling with amusement.

"Not yet. I can't decide between 'A Generous Champion' and 'He Kindly Allowed the Rest of Us to Play.'" She smiles. "Perhaps I'll settle the question by winning the next league."

title: An Unexpected Debt
text:
You encounter Emma in a quiet corridor of the Academy, standing by a window with a letter in her hands. She seems unusually still, her eyes fixed on the page. As you approach, she hastily folds the letter and slips it into her pocket. By the time she turns toward you, her familiar composure has almost returned.

"Antonio. What a pleasant surprise." Her smile is perfectly polite, and almost perfectly convincing.

You ask whether something is wrong.

"Nothing worth troubling you with." She looks away, then lets out a quiet sigh. "Oh, very well. It seems my bank has developed an exciting new interpretation of our agreement. One in which I owe them rather a lot of money, rather sooner than expected."

She attempts a dismissive smile, but it doesn't quite work. "I borrowed the money to pay my tuition. I've been working towards a place here for years, and I thought I had everything arranged." She pauses, looking through the window at the Academy grounds. "If I cannot meet their demand, I may have to leave."

For a moment, she seems very far away. Then she straightens her shoulders.

"Well. I've faced worse difficulties." Her voice regains some of its customary firmness. "I'll find a solution. I always do."

parameters.title: Academy education financed through a loan
parameters.description: Emma's Academy education is financed through a loan. Her family's circumstances have made her education difficult to afford, and remaining at the Academy is extremely important to her.

optionTemplates.text: Offer to lend her the money

parameters.text:
"I have some savings," you say. "Not much, but perhaps enough to help you through this."

Emma looks at you, genuinely startled.

"Antonio, no. Absolutely not."

You insist that you're serious.

"I can see that." Her expression softens. "And I can also see that you're hardly in a position to throw money around. You worked for your place here too, didn't you?"

She hesitates, evidently searching for the right words.

"That's an extraordinarily generous offer. And an extraordinarily foolish one." A faint smile appears. "Please don't make me choose between accepting your kindness and calling you an idiot."

She reaches out and briefly squeezes your arm.

"Thank you. Truly. But this is my problem to solve."

"Antonio," Emma says, unusually quiet, "I've never properly thanked you for offering me your savings when the bank caused all that trouble." You tell her she already did. "Then consider this an academic revision." She meets your eyes. "It was a ridiculous offer. Generous, reckless, quite possibly catastrophic for you." A small smile returns. "I was very glad you made it. And I'm still glad I refused."

"Actually, I might have a solution. Molly is looking for someone to tutor children from the village. It's paid work, and you'd be perfect for it."

Emma considers this. "Molly? Yes, I know about her little project. But why me?"

"Why you? Emma, you're probably the brightest student in the Academy. You understand things in an afternoon that take the rest of us weeks. You're disciplined, articulate, extraordinarily well-read, and you have this remarkable ability to—"

You stop.

Emma is looking at you with an expression of delighted fascination. One eyebrow rises slowly.

"Please, don't stop on my account. I was particularly enjoying the part about my extraordinary abilities."

"Yes, well. I meant that you're qualified for the position."

"Naturally." Her smile grows. "Please continue. I believe you were about to mention my devastating intellect."

You decide that the less you say, the better.

Fortunately, Emma's attention returns to the opportunity itself. "Actually, it's a wonderful idea. I could arrange the hours around my studies, and Molly would certainly be reasonable about the pay. Why didn't I think of this before?"

She's already halfway down the corridor when she suddenly stops, turns around, and hurries back.

"Antonio."

She takes your hand in both of hers and looks you directly in the eyes. The teasing expression has vanished, replaced by something unusually earnest.

"Thank you. Truly."

For a brief moment, neither of you speaks. Then she releases your hand, gives you a brilliant smile, and rushes off in search of Molly.

You suspect the subject of your little speech has not been forgotten. Not remotely.

"Molly's tutoring arrangement was an excellent suggestion," Emma says. "Though I confess I remember something else about that conversation." You brace yourself. "Your assessment of my extraordinary intelligence. My discipline. My incomparable suitability for the position." You begin to protest. "Please, Antonio, don't become modest now. You were making such a persuasive argument. I nearly hired myself on the spot."

text:
Professor Glützenbaum enters the classroom with a letter in his hand and an expression suggesting that someone has committed a grave offense against civilization. He marches to his lectern, waits for silence, and adjusts his spectacles.

"Students. I have received an invitation from the Royal College of Artificery of Falkenstein. They are organizing a competition for first-year students, in which each participating Academy will send two representatives to demonstrate their talents in card crafting and tournament play."

A murmur of excitement runs through the room. Glützenbaum raises his hand.

"Allow me to read their invitation."

He clears his throat. "'It would give us the greatest pleasure to welcome representatives of your venerable institution, whose dedication to preserving the traditional methods of artificery is widely appreciated.'"

He pauses. His left eyebrow twitches.

"'While we recognize that certain provincial academies may lack access to the most recent advances in our discipline, we firmly believe that exposure to the standards of our leading institutions can only benefit their promising young scholars.'"

The room goes very quiet.

"'We therefore warmly encourage your participation, regardless of the eventual results, in the spirit of academic fellowship and mutual enrichment.'"

Glützenbaum lowers the letter.

"**Regardless of the eventual results.**"

He lets the words hang in the air.

"These pompous, silk-robed, overfunded—" He stops, straightens his spectacles, and takes a breath. "These esteemed colleagues appear to have forgotten that some of the finest artificers in the history of the discipline received their education within these very walls!"

The classroom erupts. Molly, usually so reserved, is on her feet, punching the air with both fists and cheering enthusiastically. Ousmane leans back in his chair, slowly twirling his magnificent moustache with the expression of a general contemplating a particularly satisfying campaign. Farid has produced a small knife and is flipping it expertly between his fingers, apparently considering the matter settled in favor of hostilities.

Someone at the back of the room shouts, "We'll show them!" Several others take up the cry. Glützenbaum makes a token attempt to restore order, but his heart is plainly not in it.

"Quite right!" he thunders, then remembers himself. "That is to say, we shall respond with the utmost dignity, professionalism, and devastating academic superiority!"

He strikes the lectern with his palm. A small cloud of chalk dust rises dramatically.

"Now! Each institution must appoint a captain, who will select a second student. I have given this matter considerable thought, and our captain shall be Miss Emma Delamain."

There is an enthusiastic round of applause. Emma rises gracefully from her seat, accepting the nomination with a composed smile that nevertheless betrays a certain fierce satisfaction.

"Thank you, Professor. I shall endeavor to make the Academy proud."

"I have every confidence that you will, Miss Delamain. And whom would you choose as your partner?"

"Antonio Fibonacci."

She answers without a moment's hesitation. You look up. A few heads turn in your direction.

Glützenbaum nods thoughtfully. "An interesting choice. Are you quite certain?"

"Entirely."

She turns toward you, her expression now wearing that familiar mixture of amusement and challenge.

"Unless, of course, Antonio has suddenly developed an objection to winning."

You have scarcely begun to formulate a response when Glützenbaum claps his hands.

"Excellent! Delamain and Fibonacci shall represent us. You have one week to prepare. I expect discipline, ingenuity, and above all, a performance that will make our distinguished colleagues regret having learned to write letters!"

The room bursts into applause once more. Ousmane rises to shake your hand with great solemnity. Molly beams at you from across the classroom. Farid gives you an approving nod and, mercifully, puts away his knife.

As the students begin to disperse, Emma approaches you with the purposeful stride of someone whose campaign has already begun.

"Tomorrow evening. My room. Bring your best deck, your crafting notes, and any ideas you consider worth defending. We have a great deal of work ahead of us."

"Do I get any say in this?"

"Certainly. You may choose whether to arrive at seven or disappoint me."

She gives you a wicked little smile.

"And Antonio? Do try to get some rest tonight. I intend to be extremely demanding."

With that, she sweeps out of the classroom, leaving you to contemplate the peculiar honor of having been recruited into Emma Delamain's personal war against the Royal College of Falkenstein.

text:
Emma's lodgings occupy a modest room on the upper floor of a rustic village inn. A narrow bed stands against one wall, a battered armchair occupies the other, and nearly every remaining surface has been conquered by books. A small kettle steams beside two cups on the desk. Apparently, your arrival has been anticipated with military precision.

"Seven o'clock. Excellent." Emma opens the door wider. "I was beginning to wonder whether I'd need to send a search party."

{{ greeting }}

She leads you to the desk, where two decks lie beside a rather alarming collection of tournament regulations, strategic diagrams, and handwritten notes. Evidently, Emma has not spent the afternoon idle.

"We have a few evenings before Falkenheim, and a great deal to accomplish. Unfortunately, time is a resource even I haven't yet learned to manufacture." She points to two piles of documents. "So we must choose our priorities."

"We could study our opponents, learn how they play, and prepare something unpleasant for them. Or we could concentrate on our own performance and spend tonight practicing against each other."

She smiles, with the dangerous enthusiasm of someone who considers both possibilities excellent entertainment.

"Well, partner? How shall we spend our evening?"

parameters.text:
"If we know how they play, we can prepare a counter-strategy. Why fight them on their terms?"

"An excellent principle." Emma considers the tournament invitation again. "And I believe I know where we might begin."

Her expression brightens with a rather mischievous idea.

"Elsa Falkenstein."

"We know our own decks better than theirs. Let's put that advantage to work. A few practice games should reveal where we need improvement."

"Splendid." Emma pushes the documents aside and begins arranging her cards.

"Although I must warn you, Antonio, I have no intention of going easy on you merely because we're on the same team."

You wouldn't dream of asking.

Emma explains that Elsa Falkenstein comes from Falkenheim itself, and that her older brother is widely regarded as the Royal College's most promising first-year student.

"He's almost certainly their captain. And Elsa knows him rather well, as siblings unfortunately tend to."

"Then we should ask her."

"Yes." Emma purses her lips. "There's just one small complication."

She reminds you of that unfortunate incident at the ballet, when Elsa attempted to make a spectacle of her and ended up providing the entertainment herself.

"I doubt she's forgiven me. Which is rather unfair, since I wasn't the one who arranged the whole thing."

A short walk brings you to Elsa's lodgings, in an inn whose polished marble entrance and liveried servants suggest an establishment considerably more prosperous than Emma's. Elsa receives you in a beautifully furnished sitting room, where she listens to your explanation with growing amusement.

"So. The illustrious Emma Delamain has come to ask for _my_ assistance."

"Information, Elsa. Not divine intervention."

"How disappointing. I was rather looking forward to the latter."

Elsa settles into her upholstered chair, crossing one leg elegantly over the other.

"My brother is an exceptional player. I know his preferred cards, his strategies, even his latest decklist." She smiles. "But why, exactly, should I share any of that with you?"

Positively alarming." She considers the matter. "Still, we obtained the information we needed." You suggest that a bill eventually comes due. "Yes, yes. Do stop introducing economics into a perfectly pleasant conversation."

She stops.

You smile.

Emma's expression becomes one of profound appreciation.

"Elsa," she says gently, "I believe Antonio was asking a question."

Elsa stares at you both.

"I despise clever people."

"An unfortunate prejudice," Emma replies, "particularly at an Academy."

You continue the conversation, carefully encouraging Elsa to correct your increasingly inaccurate guesses about her brother's strategy. Eventually, exasperated by your apparent ignorance, she snatches a sheet of paper from her desk.

"Oh, for heaven's sake. Here! This is his decklist. Perhaps you'll understand what I'm talking about when you see it."

Emma accepts the document with a gracious smile.

"How very instructive. Thank you, Elsa."

It is only as you rise to leave that Elsa seems to reconsider the entire conversation.

"Wait a moment..."

"I still think of the expression on Elsa's face when she realized she'd handed us that decklist," Emma says, visibly delighted. "All you had to do was be confidently wrong until she couldn't resist correcting you." You call it a sophisticated intelligence-gathering technique. "Naturally. A triumph of strategic incompetence. I've been tempted to try it on Professor Glützenbaum, though I suspect he'd simply give us a lecture."

You begin probing Elsa's knowledge with what you consider a series of subtle questions.

Unfortunately, Elsa proves rather less susceptible to subtlety than you'd hoped.

"Antonio, darling, if you want to know my brother's strategy, you could simply ask." She smiles. "I would still refuse, naturally, but we'd save ourselves so much time."

Emma hides a smile behind her hand.

"An admirable attempt, Fibonacci. Perhaps we should try a less elaborate approach."

She turns to Elsa, her expression becoming unusually serious.

"All right. What would it take for you to give us that decklist?"

Elsa arches an eyebrow.

"Are you offering to beg?"

"Don't be absurd. I'm offering you a favor. From both of us, whenever you might need it."

You turn toward Emma, rather alarmed by the sudden generosity of this proposal.

Elsa, meanwhile, looks as though someone has just presented her with a particularly magnificent birthday gift.

"Both of you?" She studies you in turn, her smile widening. "My dear Emma, I had no idea you could be so accommodating."

"Do you accept or not?"

"Oh, absolutely."

She opens a drawer, retrieves a folded sheet, and hands it to Emma with considerable ceremony.

"One complete decklist, as requested. And two exceptionally talented Academy students owing me a favor. What a delightful afternoon."

On the way back, you finally manage to interrupt Emma's enthusiastic examination of the document.

"Emma. About that favor..."

"Yes?"

"We have absolutely no idea what Elsa is going to ask us to do."

"No."

"And you don't find that concerning?"

Emma looks up at you, apparently surprised.

"Antonio, we have the decklist. We can worry about everything else after we've won."

You are beginning to suspect that Emma Delamain's attitude toward risk depends rather heavily on whether she considers the objective sufficiently glorious.

"I've reviewed your attempt to coax the decklist out of Elsa," Emma says. "A daring plan. Unfortunately, she noticed it before the second question." You remind her they got the information anyway. "Yes, at the modest price of a favor whose terms we don't know." She sighs. "If Elsa ever asks us to perform at one of her parties, I'm blaming you."

investigate_opposition.title: Know Your Enemy

practice_session.text:
The first game begins innocently enough.

Within minutes, Emma is leaning over the table, studying your cards with the concentration of a chess master contemplating the invasion of a small country. She makes no secret of her pleasure whenever she finds a weakness in your defenses, and considerably less of her displeasure when you exploit one of hers.

One game becomes three. Then five. You experiment with unfamiliar openings, exchange decks to understand each other's strengths, and argue over the merits of various strategies with increasing enthusiasm.

At some point, Emma forgets to pour the tea. At another, she forgets to drink it.

By the time the innkeeper knocks to ask whether you intend to order supper, both of you have become quite determined to win the next game.

parameters.text:
The final game is a masterpiece of accumulated cunning. Emma anticipates your opening, you anticipate her response, and the two of you spend several turns laying traps for someone who is doing precisely the same thing.

Then you spot an opportunity.

Emma studies the board, narrows her eyes, and slowly looks up at you.

"Oh, that is _vile_."

You make your move.

She stares at the cards for another moment, then throws back her head and laughs.

"Well played, Antonio. Infuriatingly well played."

"I believe that's what they call a compliment."

"Don't become accustomed to it. I intend to rectify the situation at the earliest opportunity."

"I've found a defense against that vile move you played during our tournament practice," Emma announces. You ask whether she's certain. "Absolutely. I've tested it six times." You suggest a seventh. "How very helpful." Her eyes brighten. "Actually, yes. Bring your deck. I should hate for you to imagine that one moment of inspired wickedness confers permanent superiority."

For a glorious moment, you believe you have her cornered.

Then Emma plays a card you had entirely forgotten was in her deck.

You examine the board. You examine your hand. You examine the board again, in the faint hope that one of its features might have changed out of courtesy.

"Checkmate," Emma announces.

"Wrong game."

"An insignificant technicality." She leans back with a triumphant smile. "Would you like me to explain where you went wrong?"

"Would you enjoy that?"

"Immensely."

She does, however, spend the next several minutes explaining her winning combination, and together you identify several adjustments that could strengthen your tournament decks.

"Checkmate," Emma says without looking up from her cards. You remind her, once again, that this isn't chess. "And yet the result was unmistakable, wasn't it?" She gives you an immaculate smile. "I've also been thinking about the sequence that won our last practice match. There was a rather elegant combination in it. Would you care to hear the explanation again?"

"I found a cup of tea behind my notes this morning," Emma says. "I believe it dates from our tournament practice session." You ask whether she drank it. "Antonio, even I'm not that devoted to scholarship." She smiles at the memory. "We played so long the innkeeper nearly had to remind us that meals exist. An excellent evening. Entirely unreasonable, of course, but excellent."

practice_session.title: Practice Makes Perfect

training_conclusion.text:
{{ preparation_recap }}

It is now quite late. The village has grown quiet outside the windows, and the innkeeper has extinguished most of the lights downstairs. Emma tidies the table with practiced efficiency, gathering the scattered notes and cards into neat piles.

"Well. I think we've made excellent progress."

She pours the last of the tea, discovers that it is cold, and drinks it anyway.

"There's one final question we should settle."

She retrieves the tournament regulations.

"Two matches. I'll face Falkenheim's captain, and you'll face their second. If we win one each, there will be a deciding match. We must nominate which of us will play it."

{{ finalist_preference }}

She sets down the regulations and looks at you.

"What do you think, Antonio? Which of us should have the honor?"

parameters.text:
"I'll take it. Whatever happens in the first two matches, I want to be the one who settles the score."

Emma studies you for a moment, then smiles.

"Very well. I hope you appreciate the magnitude of the responsibility you've just volunteered to assume."

"I thought you wanted someone ambitious."

"I do. But ambition without competence is merely a particularly entertaining form of self-destruction."

She extends her hand.

"Don't disappoint me, Fibonacci."

You shake it.

"Wouldn't dream of it. See you in a couple of days to craft an amazing card!"

optionTemplates.text: Let Emma take the deciding match

parameters.text:
"You're the captain. And I trust you to handle the final if it comes to that."

Emma regards you thoughtfully.

"How remarkably sensible of you."

"Try not to sound so surprised."

"I'm doing my best."

She smiles, but there's genuine appreciation behind the teasing.

"Very well. I'll take the deciding match. You concentrate on beating their second, and leave the other one to me."

She offers her hand across the table.

"Agreed?"

"Agreed. . See you in a couple of days to craft an amazing card!"

training_conclusion.title: The Deciding Match

variants.text:
Back in Emma's room, you spread Elsa's precious decklist across the table. It is an intimidating collection of aggressive creatures, sacrificial combinations, and devastating offensive abilities.

Emma studies it in silence, occasionally making a small annotation.

"Interesting. Very interesting. He clearly favors overwhelming his opponents before they can establish themselves."

She begins arranging cards into groups.

"Look at these units. Fast, cheap, dangerous... but almost none of them can survive a proper hit."

She sits back, her eyes brightening.

"Antonio, I think I've found something."

She points to the fragile creatures that form the backbone of the opposing deck.

"A single powerful defender wouldn't help us. He could simply overwhelm it. But a spell that strikes _every_ enemy unit at once, even for a modest amount of damage..."

You look again at the decklist.

"Would wipe out most of his forces."

"Precisely!"

Emma smiles with the fierce satisfaction of someone who has just discovered a particularly elegant solution to an unpleasant problem.

"We need a cheap spell that damages several units simultaneously. Something we can deploy before his offensive gets out of hand."

She takes a fresh sheet of parchment and begins sketching possibilities.

"I think, Antonio, that we have just discovered what we'll be crafting together."

You finish reviewing the evening's games, including your particularly satisfying final victory. Emma is still disputing one of your moves, although her argument has gradually shifted from claiming it was unsound to complaining that she hadn't thought of it first.

"Some of your combinations were genuinely clever," she admits. "I've been making notes. If I can incorporate a few of those ideas into my own play, Falkenheim may find me a rather unpleasant opponent."

You finish reviewing the evening's games. Emma has won the final encounter, a fact she has mentioned only three times in the last quarter of an hour.

"Your defense improved considerably toward the end," she observes. "And you forced me to reconsider several combinations I thought I knew perfectly well."

She smiles.

"I believe the evening has been most educational. For both of us."

preparation_recap.fallback: You finish reviewing your preparation notes together. There is still much to do before the tournament, but at least you now have a clearer idea of what lies ahead.

variants.text:
"I've considered it carefully," Emma says. "Given your performance in the last league, I think you ought to take the deciding match."

She delivers this judgment with perfect composure, though you suspect conceding the point has cost her something.

"Don't look so astonished, Fibonacci. I can recognize superior results when they are placed directly under my nose."

She smiles.

"Besides, I intend to win my own match. With any luck, you won't be needed."

finalist_preference.fallback:
"I propose that I take the deciding match," Emma says. "I've been preparing for this competition rather obsessively, and I believe I'm our strongest choice."

She pauses, then adds more thoughtfully:

"But you're my partner, not my subordinate. If you see it differently, I'm willing to hear your argument."

text:
The Academy's artificery room is deserted at this hour, its great wooden tables and elaborate magical instruments illuminated by the last rays of evening sunlight. Emma has already prepared a workspace when you arrive, complete with ingredients, drafting tools, and two cups of something hot.

"Excellent timing, Antonio. I've managed to borrow the room for the evening, and I intend to make the most of it."

{{ crafting_plan }}

The work begins with the usual disagreements. Emma favors precision, careful calculations, and meticulous preparation. You suggest a few rather less orthodox solutions, which she initially regards with suspicion before reluctantly admitting that some of them have merit. Soon, however, the arguments give way to an easy rhythm. You begin anticipating each other's ideas, correcting mistakes before they happen, and occasionally arriving at the same conclusion simultaneously.

"Remarkable," Emma observes after one such coincidence. "We're beginning to think alike. I do hope this isn't permanent."

At last, everything is ready. The two of you stand opposite each other across the crafting table, hands extended toward the unfinished card. As your magical auras flow into the ritual, the familiar patterns of energy begin to form, then unexpectedly intertwine, circling one another in a luminous spiral.

For a moment, the entire room seems to hold its breath.

A brilliant flash illuminates the table, and the ritual ends.

Where there should have been a single creation, two identical cards now rest side by side.

Emma picks one up, examines its magical properties, and breaks into a delighted smile.

"It worked! Antonio, look at this. The balance is excellent, the enchantment is stable, and the duplication is absolutely flawless!"

She turns the card over.

Her smile freezes.

"That's... unusual."

You examine the second card. The illustration depicts the two of you together, surrounded by the magical forces you've just summoned. Emma stands close beside you, one hand resting naturally on your shoulder, while the two figures exchange a look of complete and effortless trust.

The resemblance is unmistakable. The intimacy, rather less expected.

"Is that supposed to be us?"

"Apparently." Emma examines the image with scholarly concentration. "How curious. Conjured illustrations aren't supposed to depict living people, much less their creators."

She tilts the card toward the light.

"The likeness is remarkably good, though."

{{ antonio_reaction }}

{{ emma_reaction }}

Emma places the two cards side by side, apparently determined to return to safer intellectual territory.

"Well, whatever caused this anomaly, the result is excellent. And there are two of them, so naturally we shall keep one each."

"Which one's mine?"

She studies the cards for a moment.

"An excellent question."

"You don't know?"

"Of course I know. I'm simply deciding whether you deserve the better one."

She hands you a card, keeping the other for herself. They are, as far as either of you can determine, perfectly identical.

For a moment, you both regard your newly acquired creations with considerable satisfaction.

parameters.text:
"I must say, the card has captured my heroic qualities rather well. Your presence is a nice addition, of course."

Emma looks at you with an expression of exquisite disbelief.

"Your heroic qualities?"

"Quite unmistakable."

"Antonio, I'm fairly certain I'm the one performing the difficult magic in that picture. You appear to be providing moral support."

"An indispensable contribution."

"Naturally. I'll be sure to mention it when they erect your statue."

She turns the card over again, a mischievous smile spreading across her face.

"Though I must admit, the artist has been rather generous with your jawline."

Emma turns her copy of your joint creation toward you. "I've reconsidered your role in this portrait." You straighten expectantly. "Moral support," she declares. "An essential contribution, clearly. The magic was mine; the heroic jawline, apparently, yours." You ask whether she still thinks the portrait flattering. "Oh, certainly. Particularly given how generously the artist treated your face."

"You know, Emma, I rather like it. Not just the card. The two of us working together."

Emma looks at you, then at the illustration.

"Yes," she says after a moment. "I think I do too."

She turns the card slowly between her fingers.

"I've always preferred working alone. It's generally more efficient, and one has fewer people to disappoint." She gives you a brief, amused glance. "But I must concede that having someone capable beside me has its advantages."

"High praise."

"Don't let it go to your head."

Her smile softens.

"Seriously, Antonio. We do make a good team."

"I've been looking at our matching cards again," Emma says. "Not the enchantment this time. The two of us." She pauses, then gives you a small smile. "I meant what I said that evening. I've always worked better alone—or thought I did." You remind her that collaboration has advantages. "Don't become insufferable about it, Fibonacci. But yes. Some advantages are rather difficult to deny."

"I must say, the artist has excellent taste in couples."

Emma raises an eyebrow.

"Couples? How very forward of you, Fibonacci. I wasn't aware we'd progressed beyond an academic partnership."

"I'm merely appreciating the artistic interpretation."

"Naturally." She studies the illustration again. "And here I thought we were crafting a tournament card, not commissioning a romantic portrait."

"Perhaps the magic knows something we don't."

"An alarming possibility. Though I should warn you, Antonio, magical phenomena are notoriously unreliable when it comes to matters of the heart."

She gives you a wicked little smile.

"Still, I suppose there are worse people to be immortalized alongside."

You decide to accept the compliment before she has time to reconsider it.

"I've had another look at our famous portrait," Emma says. "The magic still seems convinced we're a very handsome couple." You ask whether she disagrees. "I'm questioning its methodology, Antonio. Artistic enchantments are not a recognized authority on matters of the heart." She studies your expression. "Though I'll concede its taste in company could be considerably worse."

text:
Falkenheim School greets you with polished marble, towering statues, and the sort of silence that makes you reluctant to breathe too loudly. Apparently, wealth can buy almost everything except a welcoming atmosphere.

The school's director offers a stiff greeting to your delegation. Beside him stands Franz Falkenstein, Elsa's older brother and Falkenheim's team captain: handsome, impeccably dressed, and evidently aware of both facts. His second, Olga Saratovskaya, is a tall, pale young woman with almost white-blond hair and icy blue eyes. She surveys you with the faint, cruel interest of someone inspecting a particularly disappointing specimen.

Emma draws Franz for the opening round. You draw Olga.

"Try not to look so frightened, Antonio," Emma murmurs. "I'm sure she doesn't actually eat her opponents. And do stop glaring at Franz. He's not _that_ handsome."

parameters.text: Olga takes her seat without a greeting, arranges her cards with surgical precision, and fixes you with a chilly stare. You shuffle your deck and try to look like someone who has never been intimidated in his life.

text:
"Can you believe them? All airs and graces until someone gives them a proper thrashing, and then their true colors come out! Miserable scoundrels! Blackguards! Unspeakable little weasels!"

Well. You've never seen Emma quite like this. Your impeccably mannered, perpetually composed Emma, apparently equipped with an entire vocabulary of insults you've never heard her use before. You make a mental note never to get on her bad side.

{{flushedCheeks}}

"Don't worry, Emma. We'll figure something out," you assure her, cradling a trophy so enormous that the sight of you carrying it is becoming faintly ridiculous.

"Of course we'll figure something out. But without any money, we'll need to be a little inventive. Perhaps—"

Emma stops. Her gaze settles on a farmer's cart, piled high with vegetables, trundling toward the city gates in the direction of the Academy.

"Ah, yes," she mutters. "The triumphant return of the conquering heroes."

She motions for you to stay put and strides toward the driver.

Half a minute later, she beckons you over. The farmer has apparently agreed to take her along for free. Judging by the look of wonder on his face, this has required remarkably little persuasion.

The wonder fades into resignation when he sees you approaching, trophy and all.

"Right, you two. I'll take you to that school of whatever-it-is, but I've got two conditions. First, no funny business in my cart! I know what you young lovebirds are like."

Emma draws herself up, visibly outraged. Unfortunately for her, you recover first.

"Not to worry, sir. My wife is perfectly capable of controlling her passions. Most of the time."

Emma turns very slowly toward you.

You'll pay for that later. Absolutely worth it.

"And second," the farmer continues, pointing his thumb at a mountainous stack of crates, "you help me load up."

parameters.text:
"I'll handle the crates. Emma, could you look into how we collect our prize money?"

Emma's expression darkens at the first sentence.

"Of course you are. But I suspect the tournament regulations are considerably more complicated than a pile of vegetables, and I'd rather leave the difficult part to you."

She considers this, then gives an approving nod.

"A sensible division of labor, Fibonacci. You may yet have a future in management."

She retrieves the tournament documents while you set about discovering precisely how many vegetables one farmer can own.

"Of course! Come along, darling. A little honest work will do us both good."

"Keep calling me that, Fibonacci, and I'll give you some honest work to remember."

Nevertheless, she rolls up her sleeves and joins you. Between the two of you, the crates disappear into the cart at a respectable pace, accompanied by increasingly inventive threats concerning your immediate future.

The farmer watches the exchange with a knowing smile.

"Young love," he remarks.

Emma nearly drops a cabbage.

The farmer examines it, scratches his beard, and asks whether it's made of real gold.

Emma closes her eyes. You decide this is an excellent moment to start lifting crates.

A little later, as you wrestle with a particularly stubborn sack of potatoes, Emma murmurs, "The heroes of Falkenheim. Defeated by root vegetables."

title: The Road Home

variants.text: Although, you have to admit, the flushed cheeks rather suit her.

the_champions_return.text:
"Ah."

You and Emma stare into the back of the cart.

It is packed to the brim with vegetables. There is barely room for two people, let alone two people and a trophy the size of a small child. Emma, who has been gazing at the latter with undisguised affection ever since the award ceremony, suddenly seems rather less enamored of it.

"Would you prefer to sit on the carrots or the potatoes, darling?"

"Oh, give it a rest. He can't hear you anymore."

"I know, my love."

Emma rolls her eyes and climbs aboard.

To your surprise, she reveals a remarkable talent for logistics. Within moments, a few crates have been shifted, several sacks rearranged, and a small, reasonably comfortable nest has emerged between a wall of cabbages and a heap of apples.

She settles into it, draws her knees up, and pats the floor beside her.

The smile on her face suggests that revenge is imminent.

"Don't be shy, sweetheart."

Oh, no.

Forty centimeters. At most.

You swallow and sit down as far from her as physically possible, which turns out to mean pressed firmly against her side, with the enormous trophy balanced across your knees.

"Not going to faint on me, are you, Fibonacci?"

You brace yourself for several hours of merciless teasing.

But, unexpectedly, Emma merely gives you a peaceful little smile. The cart lurches forward, and she turns to watch the countryside roll past.

No sarcastic remarks. No clever observations at your expense.

Well.

Here you are, then.

Lovely weather, isn't it?

And, er...

Oh, for heaven's sake, _say something._

You risk a glance at Emma. She's watching the distant hills, looking almost dreamy. Several minutes pass. She doesn't appear troubled by the silence in the slightest.

Then she turns toward you.

Quick. Think of something.

But she only smiles, very slightly, before looking away again.

Eventually, she takes a book from her bag and begins reading. Every now and then, she comes across a passage she particularly enjoys and reads it aloud to you, supplying a scholarly commentary that is considerably longer than the passage itself.

Naturally, this also presents opportunities to remind you that a little more reading would do you a world of good.

The hours slip by. The afternoon light softens. The sun sinks toward the horizon.

After the madness of the past week, exhaustion begins to catch up with you.

You really ought to stay awake. It would be terribly embarrassing to—

When you open your eyes again, it is dark.

Someone has tucked a blanket around you.

That's... rather nice, actually.

Wait.

Something isn't quite right.

Your head.

Oh.

{{shoulderRealization}}

Very slowly, you lift it. Straighten your back. Fix your eyes on the darkness ahead.

Whatever you do, don't look at her.

The cart rattles to a stop.

"Sleep well?"

Emma is pressing her lips together, plainly struggling not to laugh.

Mercifully, she says nothing more.

"Come on. We're here."

parameters.text:
You climb down from the cart, grateful for the darkness concealing your expression. Emma follows, stretches her stiff legs, and thanks the farmer with considerably more warmth than she showed the Falkenheim organizers.

Then she looks at you, at the trophy, and at the Academy's distant lights.

"Well, Fibonacci. One last heroic effort."

You pick up the trophy.

Of course.

the_champions_return.title: The Champions' Triumphant Return

variants.text:
Oh, no.

With a peculiar mixture of overwhelming happiness and mortal terror, you realize you've been sleeping with your head resting on Emma's shoulder.

shoulderRealization.fallback:
You've been sleeping with your head resting on Emma's shoulder.

a_practical_arrangement.text:
By the time you've carried the trophy into the Academy's entrance hall, the night is well advanced. You set it down beneath the chandeliers, where it looks almost respectable again.

"Well, Fibonacci," Emma says, surveying it with satisfaction. "That's one thing successfully accomplished."

"Yes. I think we've earned ourselves a little rest."

Emma gives you a questioning look, as though the word _rest_ belongs to some obscure foreign language.

But then her expression changes.

"Listen, Antonio. I wanted to..."

She pauses, her gaze drifting toward the trophy, where both your names are engraved.

"I wanted to thank you. I don't know if I could have won without you."

There's an unfamiliar softness in her eyes. For an instant, you wonder if they might even be a little damp.

No. Not Emma. Must be the candlelight.

"You would have found a way," you tell her. "You always do."

"Perhaps." She smiles faintly. "But I'm rather glad I didn't have to."

She looks back at the engraved names.

"My parents gave everything they could to help me enter that tournament," she says quietly. "So I rather had to win."

For a moment, she says nothing more. You can almost see the familiar calculations turning behind her eyes: expenses, expectations, obligations, all the things she never quite manages to put aside.

Then she takes a breath, and something of her usual energy returns.

"You know what, Antonio? We make far too good a team to leave it at that. How about a regular study evening? My place, every Tuesday?"

She tilts her head, already adopting the air of someone presenting an entirely sensible academic proposal.

"It would be mutually beneficial, obviously. We could review our crafting techniques, compare strategies, perhaps work on a few new cards. There's no reason to let such a productive partnership go to waste."

Her eyes are smiling.

"Good."

The word comes out a little too quickly. She clears her throat.

"Excellent, then. Tuesdays, seven o'clock. Bring your books, and do try to arrive with something useful between your ears."

She starts toward the stairs, then pauses.

"And Antonio? I did enjoy working with you."

Before you can answer, she adds, "Despite the considerable disadvantages."

There she is.

title: The Road Home — Defeat Route
text:
The carriage rolls out of Falkenheim beneath a grey afternoon sky.

At least the organizers have had the decency to provide transportation home. You and Emma sit opposite each other on comfortable upholstered benches, surrounded by a silence considerably less comfortable than the seats.

Emma has been staring out of the window for the better part of twenty minutes.

"Well," she says at last. "That was humiliating."

You consider pointing out that you made it remarkably far in a tournament filled with some of the Academy's finest players. Unfortunately, Emma has already begun a detailed reconstruction of your defeat.

"If I'd played the third turn differently... No, that wouldn't have worked either. Unless we'd changed the opening sequence. Or perhaps—"

"Emma."

"—if we'd anticipated their counterspell, we could have—"

"Emma."

She turns toward you.

"What?"

"The tournament's over."

She gives you a look that suggests this is an exceptionally unhelpful observation.

"Yes, Fibonacci. I had noticed."

"And we lost."

"Thank you. Do go on. Your analysis is fascinating."

"And we're still here."

Emma opens her mouth, then closes it.

You gesture vaguely between the two of you.

"We're both alive. We learned a few things. We even made some rather good cards. All things considered, I think we could have done worse."

She looks at you for a moment.

"That is a remarkably generous interpretation of events."

"One of my many talents."

"Alongside losing tournaments?"

"Especially that one."

Despite herself, she lets out a short laugh.

It's not much, but it's the first time she's smiled since the final match.

Emma considers that.

"True. Our preparation was rather effective, all things considered."

"Rather effective?"

"Don't fish for compliments, Fibonacci. It's undignified."

But she smiles again, and this time it lasts.

optionTemplates.text: Promise to do better next time

parameters.text:
"Well, there's only one thing to do now."

Emma raises an eyebrow.

"Which is?"

"Come back next year and make them regret ever learning to play."

Her eyes brighten.

"Now _that_ is a sensible proposal."

She settles back against her seat, already looking considerably more like herself.

"And this time, Fibonacci, we're going to prepare properly."

You stare at her.

"What exactly would you call the last few weeks?"

"An encouraging preliminary effort."

optionTemplates.text: Suggest that she deserves a break

parameters.text:
"You know, Emma, I think you've earned the right to be disappointed. But you might also have earned an afternoon without thinking about cards."

She looks genuinely perplexed.

"What would I think about instead?"

"The scenery? The weather? The extraordinary luxury of not having to defeat anyone for several hours?"

She glances out the window.

"Hm. I suppose the countryside is rather pretty."

A pause.

"And I suppose the company could be worse."

"High praise indeed."

"Don't let it go to your head."

the_carriage_ride.text:
The carriage follows the winding road through fields and wooded hills. Little by little, the disappointment of the tournament begins to loosen its grip.

Emma eventually puts away her notes. This alone feels like a significant achievement.

For a while, you talk about the matches, the opponents, and the rather extraordinary things people are willing to do in pursuit of a trophy. Then the conversation wanders elsewhere, and finally fades into a comfortable silence.

Emma takes a book from her bag and begins reading.

Every now and then, she shares a passage she finds interesting, followed by an explanation that assumes you possess approximately twice your actual knowledge of the subject.

"You really ought to read more, Antonio."

"You really ought to recommend shorter books."

"Philistine."

But she is smiling.

As the afternoon fades, exhaustion catches up with you. You close your eyes for what you intend to be a moment.

When you wake, the carriage is dark except for the lantern swaying above the driver's seat.

A blanket has been draped over you.

Emma is still reading, though her book rests lower in her lap now. She notices you're awake and closes it.

"Feeling better?"

"A little. How long was I asleep?"

"Long enough for me to enjoy several hours of uninterrupted intellectual peace."

"You're welcome."

She gives you a small smile.

"Actually, it was rather nice."

You aren't entirely sure whether she means the peace or the company.

Perhaps both.

The carriage slows as the Academy's lights appear ahead.

"Well," Emma says, gathering her things. "Home again."

parameters.text:
You climb down from the carriage and help Emma with her bag. She thanks the driver, then looks up at the illuminated windows of the Academy.

"Come along, Fibonacci. I believe we have some unfinished business."

"For tonight?"

"No, you idiot." She smiles. "In general."

the_carriage_ride.title: A Quiet Journey

text:
Being summoned to the administrator's office first thing in the morning is rarely a cause for celebration. You and Emma arrive with matching expressions of suspicion, although Emma has at least made an effort to look respectable.

The administrator, however, seems positively delighted.

"Ah! Our champions! Come in, come in!" He gestures toward the chairs opposite his desk. "I have some excellent news. The Academy's reputation has benefited enormously from your little expedition to Falkenheim. The Board of Governors is most pleased."

Emma exchanges a glance with you. You've never heard the words _Board of Governors_ and _pleased_ in the same sentence before.

"Ordinarily, your tournament prize would take several weeks to process. However, in recognition of the prestige you've brought us, the Academy has decided to advance the reward from its own treasury."

He produces two official-looking documents.

"Each of you may choose between a payment of one thousand coins, or a twenty-percent discount on all purchases at the Academy's materials shop for a year."

"One thousand coins?" Emma repeats.

"Indeed."

"In actual money?"

The administrator looks mildly offended. "We do occasionally conduct our affairs in actual money, Miss Delamain."

"Cash," she says immediately.

"Perhaps you'd like to consider—"

"Cash."

"Very well, then."

He makes a note, carefully avoiding your eyes.

"And there is one more thing."

From a drawer, he produces two cards and places them on the desk.

You recognize the imposing towers, elegant courtyards, and familiar spires of your own Academy. Beautifully rendered, the illustration seems almost alive with magical energy.

"A commemorative Academy land card, for each of you. Commissioned especially for our victorious representatives."

Emma picks hers up with almost reverent care.

"A land card?" She examines it from several angles. "But these are advanced enchantments! We won't even begin studying their construction until our later years."

"Quite so. Consider it an investment in the Academy's future champions."

Emma is too busy admiring her card to notice the administrator looking rather pleased with that last remark.

"And you, Mr. Fibonacci? Which reward would you prefer?"

parameters.text:
"I'll take the money, thank you."

"A sound decision," Emma says with obvious approval.

The administrator counts out your reward and presents you with a receipt requiring only three signatures.

You sign the first.

Then the second.

By the third, you begin to understand why the Academy employs so many administrators.

"I'll take the discount at the materials shop."

Emma raises an eyebrow.

"An interesting choice, Fibonacci."

"Think how much we spend on crafting materials."

"Oh, I've thought about it. Extensively." She glances at her own reward. "But I rather suspect my banker would be less enthusiastic about accepting discounted gemstones in lieu of payment."

The administrator hands you a stamped certificate.

"Twenty percent off, valid for one year. Non-transferable, non-refundable, and subject to the usual conditions."

"How many conditions?"

"Only forty-seven."

Emma looks at you with profound sympathy.

title: The Spoils of Victory

parameters.title: Financial independence
parameters.description: Her tournament prize has allowed her to repay her tuition loan, removing the immediate threat to her education.

afterPrize.text:
Outside the office, Emma stops in the corridor and looks down at the purse in her hand.

Then she laughs.

Not her usual little sarcastic laugh, either. A genuine, delighted laugh that makes a passing student turn to stare.

"Antonio. I'm going to pay it off."

"Your loan?"

"Every last coin. The bank, the interest, those dreadful letters..." She gives the purse a little shake. "All of it. Gone!"

She looks almost dizzy with relief.

"I've spent months calculating how much I owe, how much I can earn, how long I can possibly stay here. And now..."

For a moment, she seems unable to finish the sentence.

Then she looks up at you, grinning.

"I can actually afford to be a student!"

"An alarming prospect. You might have time to enjoy yourself."

"Don't be ridiculous, Fibonacci. I have far too much work to—"

She stops.

A thoughtful expression crosses her face.

"Well. Perhaps a _little_ time."

{{tutoringThanks}}

parameters.text: "I caught myself doing something quite extraordinary yesterday," Emma says. "Looking at a purchase without first calculating which meal I'd have to skip to afford it." You ask whether the Falkenheim prize has changed her habits. "Not yet. I'm not reckless." A smile breaks through. "But I might permit myself the occasional luxury. A book, perhaps. One that isn't strictly necessary."

variants.text:
"And you know, with the money I'm earning from Molly's tutoring project, I might even be able to afford a few luxuries now and then."

She says the word _luxuries_ with the cautious fascination of someone discussing a rare and potentially dangerous magical substance.

Then her expression softens.

"Speaking of which, Antonio..."

She reaches over and gives your arm a brief, affectionate squeeze.

"Thank you. For suggesting me to Molly, I mean. I don't think I ever properly thanked you for that."

"You did, actually."

"Well, I'm doing it again. Try to endure the experience."

Her smile widens.

"Come on. I'm buying you a coffee at the cafeteria."

"You're buying?"

"Yes, Fibonacci. With my own money. A truly historic occasion."

She starts down the corridor, then looks back.

"And don't get carried away. One coffee. I'm not made of money."

tutoringThanks.fallback:
She slips the purse safely into her bag, still smiling to herself.

"Well, I ought to visit the bank before my next class."

"Already?"

"Antonio, I've been dreaming of that moment for months. I'm not waiting another day."

She takes a few steps, then turns back.

"And we should celebrate properly sometime. Preferably somewhere that doesn't charge extra for a clean table."

She gives you a bright smile.

"See you later, Fibonacci!"

text:
You arrive at the artificery classroom a little early and find Emma already at her desk, reading a letter. She looks unusually pleased with herself.

"Antonio! Excellent. I was hoping to catch you before class."

She folds the letter and sets it aside.

"Have you heard about the Academy's annual ball next Saturday? Apparently, it's quite the occasion. Music, dancing, extravagant dresses, and enough distinguished guests to populate a royal court."

You have heard something about it.

"Well, I have a particular interest in one of those guests. Lord de Varenne. An elderly gentleman, enormously respected, and one of the greatest patrons of artificery in the kingdom. He's helped launch the careers of several remarkable scholars."

Her green eyes brighten with unmistakable ambition.

"An introduction could open some very interesting doors. And I intend to make a good impression."

She pauses, then gives you a mischievous smile.

"Naturally, a young lady cannot attend such an occasion without a suitable escort. And I believe I know just the gentleman."

You look around the classroom, wondering whom she has in mind.

"Don't be obtuse, Fibonacci. I'm inviting _you_."

{{ ballet_recollection }}

"So, Antonio. Would you do me the honor of accompanying me to the ball? I promise excellent company, a respectable amount of dancing, and only a modest risk of social humiliation."

She considers that last promise.

"Well. I promise to do my best."

parameters.text:
"An evening of excellent food, dancing, and the most promising artificer of our generation? How could I refuse?"

Emma beams.

"Splendid! I knew you'd recognize a good opportunity when one presented itself."

She retrieves a small notebook and makes a mark beside something she's already written.

"You've put me on a list?"

"Naturally. One must plan ahead."

She studies you for a moment, her expression growing thoughtful.

"Although there is one small matter we'll need to address."

"What matter?"

"Your wardrobe."

You glance down at your clothes.

"What's wrong with my wardrobe?"

"Nothing at all. For attending lectures, visiting the library, or digging potatoes."

She gives you a reassuring pat on the arm.

"Don't worry, Antonio. I'll take care of everything. Meet me in town tomorrow afternoon. We'll find you something suitable."

The professor enters, and Emma turns toward the front of the classroom with a perfectly innocent expression.

You have the distinct impression that you've just volunteered for considerably more than an evening of dancing.

"I'm flattered, Emma. Truly. But I think I'll have to decline."

For a moment, she looks surprised. Then she gives a small, accepting nod.

"Of course. A pity, but I understand."

She picks up her letter again, tapping it thoughtfully against the desk.

"Well, I'll simply have to make other arrangements. It would be absurd to miss such an opportunity for want of a dancing partner."

Her familiar smile returns.

"And frankly, I was being rather generous in overlooking your questionable qualifications."

"Questionable?"

"Entirely unproven on the dance floor, Fibonacci. A considerable risk."

You laugh, and she gives you a friendly little wave as the professor enters.

"Enjoy your Saturday evening, Antonio. I shall endeavor to become rich and famous in your absence."

title: An Invitation of Sorts

parameters.title: Professional ambition
parameters.description: Emma hopes to meet Lord de Varenne at the Academy ball. He is a distinguished patron of artificery whose support could greatly advance her career.

You mention dancing, formal clothes, and the general danger of embarrassing her. "Yes, those were my concerns too." She waits for your expression to change, then laughs. "Antonio, I asked you because I wanted your company. The important guests were merely an additional advantage."

She rests her chin on one hand, looking thoroughly entertained.

"After all, I remember how deeply you appreciated my ballet performance. Such an extraordinary connoisseur of the fine arts."

She pauses delicately.

"Particularly the _physique_, if memory serves. And I assure you, Antonio, I intend to look absolutely spectacular."

Her smile becomes positively wicked.

"Though you will be expected to remain capable of speech this time. We shall be in distinguished company."

"Besides, I happen to know that you're a great admirer of dancing. I remember that expression on your face when Elsa so kindly arranged our little demonstration."

She looks at you with innocent curiosity.

"Was it my technique that impressed you, I wonder? My balance? My artistic interpretation?"

Her lips twitch.

"Or were you simply overwhelmed by the beauty of classical ballet?"

She raises an eyebrow.

She smiles at the memory.

She gives a little shrug.
